title: Direct Tax Laws and International Taxation (Final P4)
description: CA Final Paper 4 under the Income-tax Act, 2025 as amended by the Finance Act 2026 (tax year 2026-27, May 2027 attempt onward): advanced PGBP and capital gains, corporate and entity taxation, TDS, procedures, GAAR, transfer pricing and international taxation.

chapters.title: Advanced Business Income (PGBP)
chapters.summary: Special PGBP provisions at Final level: depreciation planning, disallowances, payment-based deductions and the unified presumptive scheme in section 58 of the 2025 Act.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: What changes at Final level
lesson.body:
At Intermediate you computed business income line by line. At Final the examiner expects you to apply the special provisions inside a larger problem: a company deciding between tax regimes, a firm with disallowances, or a non-resident with presumptive income. The charging provision for business income is section 26 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (corresponds to section 28 of the 1961 Act).

The 2025 Act uses one **tax year** (the financial year in which income is earned) in place of the old "previous year" and "assessment year". For the May 2027 attempt the relevant period is **tax year 2026-27** (1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027).

Final-level PGBP topics you must handle quickly:
- Depreciation on block of assets, half-rate rule, additional depreciation and the effect of opting for a concessional regime.
- Disallowances for non-deduction of tax at source, cash payments and payments to related persons (corresponds to sections 40(a), 40A(2) and 40A(3) of the 1961 Act).
- Deductions allowed only on actual payment (corresponds to section 43B of the 1961 Act), including the 15/45-day rule for micro and small enterprises.
- Presumptive taxation, now unified in **section 58** of the 2025 Act (corresponds to sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE of the 1961 Act).

lesson.heading: Depreciation and payment-based deductions
lesson.body:
Depreciation is allowed on the written down value of each block (corresponds to section 32 of the 1961 Act). If an asset is put to use for less than 180 days in the year of acquisition, only half the normal rate applies. Additional depreciation of 20% of actual cost (10% if used for less than 180 days, with the balance 10% in the next year) is available for new plant and machinery used in manufacture, but not to an assessee that opts for a concessional regime such as the 22% company regime.

Format for a block:

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Opening WDV of block | xxx |
| Add: Actual cost of assets acquired | xxx |
| Less: Moneys payable on assets sold (not below nil) | (xxx) |
| WDV before depreciation | xxx |
| Depreciation: full rate on (WDV - assets used < 180 days) | xxx |
| Depreciation: half rate on assets used < 180 days | xxx |

Payment-based deductions: tax and duty, employer contribution to PF and other funds, bonus and commission to employees, interest on loans from banks and financial institutions and leave encashment are allowed only in the year of actual payment. Payment on or before the due date for filing the return of the year saves the deduction for that year. Amounts payable to a **micro or small enterprise** must be paid within the time allowed by the MSMED Act (15 days, or up to 45 days under a written agreement); otherwise the deduction moves to the year of actual payment.

lesson.heading: Disallowances that the examiner loves
lesson.body:
- **No TDS on payment to a resident**: 30% of the expenditure is disallowed; allowed in the year in which the tax is deducted and paid.
- **No TDS on payment to a non-resident**: the whole amount is disallowed until the tax is deducted and paid.
- **Cash payment above ₹10,000** to a person in a day (₹35,000 for payments to transporters for hire of goods carriages): the whole payment is disallowed.
- **Excessive payment to a related person**: the excess over fair market value is disallowed.
- **Remuneration and interest to partners**: allowed only within the limits for firms (covered in chapter 3).

Common mistake: applying the 30% rule to a non-resident payment. For non-residents the disallowance is 100%.

lesson.heading: Presumptive taxation under section 58
lesson.body:
Section 58 of the 2025 Act brings the three old presumptive schemes into one tabular provision. The substantive rules for tax year 2026-27 follow the 1961 Act schemes:

| Scheme (1961 Act reference) | Eligible person | Limit | Presumptive income |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Business (44AD) | Resident individual, HUF, firm other than LLP | Turnover up to ₹2 crore; ₹3 crore if cash receipts do not exceed 5% | 8% of turnover; 6% of turnover received through banking or digital modes |
| Profession (44ADA) | Resident individual, firm other than LLP, in specified professions | Gross receipts up to ₹50 lakh; ₹75 lakh if cash receipts do not exceed 5% | 50% of gross receipts |
| Goods carriages (44AE) | Any person owning not more than 10 goods carriages | 10 vehicles | ₹1,000 per ton of gross vehicle weight per month for heavy vehicles; ₹7,500 per month for others |

Under presumptive taxation all deductions (including depreciation) are deemed allowed; the WDV is reduced as if depreciation had been claimed. Advance tax for the business and profession schemes is payable in one instalment by 15 March.

**Worked example.** Turnover ₹1,80,00,000, of which ₹1,20,00,000 is received by account payee cheque, UPI or bank transfer and ₹60,00,000 in cash. Cash is 33% of turnover, so the limit is ₹2 crore and the assessee is eligible. Presumptive income = 6% x 1,20,00,000 + 8% x 60,00,000 = ₹12,00,000.

Common mistakes: treating an LLP or a company as eligible; using the ₹3 crore limit when cash receipts exceed 5%; claiming depreciation separately.

keyPoints: Business income is charged under section 26 of the 2025 Act (corresponds to section 28 of the 1961 Act); the period is the tax year.
Half depreciation if an asset is used for less than 180 days in the year of acquisition; additional depreciation 20% (10% if under 180 days) on new P&M for manufacturers outside concessional regimes.
No TDS: 30% disallowance for resident payees, 100% for non-resident payees.
Cash payment above ₹10,000 per person per day (₹35,000 for transporters) is fully disallowed.
Payment-based deductions are allowed if paid by the return due date; MSME dues unpaid beyond 15/45 days are allowed only in the year of payment.
Section 58 presumptive: 8%/6% of turnover (limit ₹2 crore or ₹3 crore), 50% of professional receipts (₹50 lakh or ₹75 lakh), ₹1,000 per ton or ₹7,500 per vehicle per month.

cases.title: Case: Mehra and Sons
cases.body:
Mehra and Sons is a partnership firm (not an LLP) trading in electrical goods. Its accounts are audited and the due date for its return of income for tax year 2026-27 is 31 October 2027. Net profit as per profit and loss account: **₹42,00,000**. The following items were debited:

| Item | Amount (₹) | Facts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bonus to employees for 2026-27 | 3,00,000 | Paid on 5 November 2027 |
| Purchase from a micro enterprise (supplier) | 2,40,000 | Written agreement allows 45 days; goods accepted on 10 January 2027; paid on 20 May 2027 |
| Interest on term loan from a scheduled bank | 1,20,000 | Paid on 25 September 2027 |
| Employer contribution to PF for March 2027 | 60,000 | Deposited on 10 October 2027 |

Ignore all other adjustments.

questions.prompt: Which item debited by Mehra and Sons must be added back in computing its business income for tax year 2026-27?
options: Bonus of ₹3,00,000 and purchase of ₹2,40,000 from the micro enterprise
Bonus of ₹3,00,000 only
Interest of ₹1,20,000 and PF contribution of ₹60,000
All four items
questions.explanation: Bonus was paid after the return due date (31 October 2027), so it is allowed only in tax year 2027-28. The micro enterprise was not paid within 45 days of acceptance and also not within the year, so the deduction moves to the year of payment. Bank interest and employer PF contribution were paid before the due date, so they are allowed in 2026-27.

questions.prompt: Compute the business income of Mehra and Sons for tax year 2026-27. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Net profit as per P&L | 42,00,000 |
| Add: Bonus paid after return due date | 3,00,000 |
| Add: Micro enterprise dues not paid within 45 days | 2,40,000 |
| Interest to bank and employer PF (paid before due date) | Nil |
| **Business income** | **47,40,000** |

questions.prompt: The ₹2,40,000 added back for the micro enterprise will be allowed as a deduction in tax year 2027-28, the year in which it is actually paid.
questions.explanation: The MSME rule does not deny the expense forever. It shifts the deduction to the year of actual payment, which here is tax year 2027-28 (payment on 20 May 2027).

questions.prompt: Under section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which of these persons can opt for presumptive taxation of business income at 8% or 6% of turnover?
options: A resident partnership firm that is not an LLP
A resident LLP
A private limited company
A non-resident individual
questions.explanation: The business presumptive scheme (corresponds to section 44AD of the 1961 Act) is available to a resident individual, resident HUF and resident firm other than an LLP. Companies, LLPs and non-residents are excluded.

questions.prompt: Ravi, a resident individual trader, opts for presumptive taxation under section 58. Compute his presumptive business income for tax year 2026-27. Answer in rupees.
questions.data:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Turnover received through UPI and bank transfer | 1,20,00,000 |
| Turnover received in cash | 60,00,000 |
| Total turnover | 1,80,00,000 |
questions.explanation:
Cash receipts are 33% of turnover, so the turnover limit is ₹2 crore; ₹1.8 crore is within it.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| 6% of digital turnover ₹1,20,00,000 | 7,20,000 |
| 8% of cash turnover ₹60,00,000 | 4,80,000 |
| **Presumptive income** | **12,00,000** |

questions.prompt: Sunrise Pvt Ltd (manufacturer, not opting for any concessional regime) has the following plant and machinery block (rate 15%) for tax year 2026-27. Compute total depreciation including additional depreciation for the year. Answer in rupees.
questions.data:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Opening WDV of block on 1 April 2026 | 10,00,000 |
| New machine acquired and put to use on 10 June 2026 | 4,00,000 |
| New machine acquired and put to use on 20 November 2026 | 2,00,000 |
| Sale proceeds of an old machine (sold in August 2026) | 1,50,000 |
questions.explanation:

| --- | --- |
| Opening WDV | 10,00,000 |
| Add: Additions (4,00,000 + 2,00,000) | 6,00,000 |
| Less: Sale proceeds | (1,50,000) |

The balance 10% additional depreciation on the November machine (₹20,000) is allowed in tax year 2027-28.

questions.prompt: Compute the total amount disallowed in computing business income of a resident trader for tax year 2026-27. Answer in rupees.
questions.data:
- Professional fees of ₹5,00,000 paid to a resident chartered accountant; tax was required to be deducted but was not deducted.
- Payment of ₹25,000 in cash to a supplier of goods in a single day (not a transporter); no exception applies.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| 30% of ₹5,00,000 (no TDS on resident payee) | 1,50,000 |
| Cash payment exceeding ₹10,000 in a day: whole amount | 25,000 |
| **Total disallowance** | **1,75,000** |

questions.prompt: A resident company pays ₹20,00,000 as fees for technical services to a non-resident without deducting tax at source. What is the disallowance in the tax year of payment?
options: Nil, because TDS can be paid later
questions.explanation: For payments to non-residents, the full amount is disallowed (corresponds to section 40(a)(i) of the 1961 Act). It is allowed in the year in which tax is deducted and paid. The 30% rule applies only to resident payees.

questions.prompt: Which of these are allowed only on actual payment (payment by the return due date is enough)? Select all that apply.
options: Bonus or commission to employees
Interest on a loan from a scheduled bank
Leave encashment to employees
Purchase of raw material from a large company on credit
Employer contribution to a provident fund
questions.explanation: Bonus, bank interest, leave encashment and employer contributions to funds are payment-based deductions (corresponds to section 43B of the 1961 Act). Credit purchases from a large company are allowed on accrual; only dues to micro and small enterprises carry the time-limit rule.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the unified presumptive taxation provision of the Income-tax Act, 2025 is section ___.
questions.explanation: Section 58 of the 2025 Act combines the schemes that were in sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE of the 1961 Act, in a tabular format.

questions.prompt: Dr Anita, a resident doctor, has gross receipts of ₹70,00,000 in tax year 2026-27, of which ₹2,00,000 is in cash. Can she opt for the professional presumptive scheme, and at what income?
options: Yes, presumptive income ₹35,00,000
No, because receipts exceed ₹50 lakh
Yes, presumptive income ₹5,60,000
Yes, presumptive income ₹42,00,000
questions.explanation: Cash receipts are 2.86% of gross receipts (not more than 5%), so the higher limit of ₹75 lakh applies. Presumptive income is 50% of ₹70,00,000 = ₹35,00,000.

questions.prompt: Krishna Traders (resident individual) has turnover of ₹2,60,00,000 in tax year 2026-27. Cash receipts are ₹10,00,000; the rest is received through banking channels. Actual net profit as per books is ₹11,50,000. Advise whether he can declare presumptive income under section 58, compute it, and state the consequences if he declares only the book profit.
questions.answer:
**Eligibility**

Cash receipts = ₹10,00,000 / ₹2,60,00,000 = 3.85%, which does not exceed 5%. The turnover limit is therefore ₹3 crore, and ₹2.6 crore is within it. He is eligible.

**Presumptive income**

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| 6% of ₹2,50,00,000 (banking channels) | 15,00,000 |
| 8% of ₹10,00,000 (cash) | 80,000 |
| **Presumptive income** | **15,80,000** |

**If he declares book profit of ₹11,50,000 (lower than presumptive income)**

- His income is below the presumptive rate and his total income exceeds the basic exemption limit, so he must maintain books of account and get them audited (corresponds to sections 44AB and 44AD(5) of the 1961 Act).
- If he declared presumptive income in any earlier year and now declares lower profit, he cannot opt for the scheme again for the next five tax years.

**Advice**: compare the tax on ₹15,80,000 with the tax on ₹11,50,000 plus audit cost and the five-year lock-out. Declaring the higher presumptive income avoids audit and keeps flexibility.

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of the MSME payment rule on deductions for purchases, with an example of how it shifts the deduction between tax years.
questions.answer:
- Amounts payable to a micro or small enterprise must be paid within the period allowed by section 15 of the MSMED Act: 15 days from acceptance, or up to 45 days if agreed in writing.
- If not paid within that time, the deduction is allowed only in the tax year of actual payment, even if paid before the return due date (corresponds to section 43B(h) of the 1961 Act).
- Example: goods accepted on 1 March 2027, 45-day agreement, paid on 30 April 2027. The 45 days end on 15 April 2027, so payment is late; the deduction moves from tax year 2026-27 to 2027-28.
- If paid by 15 April 2027 it would be allowed in 2026-27.
- The rule does not apply to medium enterprises or to traders who are not registered as micro or small enterprises in the relevant category.

questions.prompt: Why does a company that opts for the 22% concessional regime lose additional depreciation, and how should it treat the unabsorbed amount?
questions.answer:
- The concessional regime (corresponds to section 115BAA of the 1961 Act) is granted on the condition that the company forgoes specified incentives, including additional depreciation, deductions for specified businesses (corresponds to section 35AD) and most Chapter VI-A style profit-linked deductions.
- Depreciation is computed at normal rates only; the block WDV is reduced by the normal depreciation.
- Unabsorbed additional depreciation relating to earlier years that cannot be set off is deemed allowed: the WDV of the block is adjusted, and it cannot be carried forward against future income.
- In exam answers, recompute depreciation without the additional component before comparing the regimes.

chapters.title: Capital Gains: Special Cases, Exemptions and Business Reorganisation
chapters.summary: Final-level capital gains: deemed consideration, slump sale, buyback after Finance Act 2026, reinvestment exemptions and tax-neutral reorganisations.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Rates and holding periods for tax year 2026-27
lesson.body:
The rate structure introduced from 23 July 2024 continues under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Section numbers below are given as the corresponding 1961 Act provisions; check the 2025 Act numbering in the ICAI study material.

| Asset | Long-term if held for more than | STCG | LTCG |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Listed equity share, equity-oriented fund unit, business trust unit (STT paid) | 12 months | 20% (corresponds to s.111A) | 12.5% on gain above ₹1,25,000 (corresponds to s.112A) |
| Other listed securities | 12 months | Normal rates | 12.5% without indexation |
| Unlisted shares, land, building, other assets | 24 months | Normal rates | 12.5% without indexation (corresponds to s.112) |

A resident individual or HUF transferring land or building acquired before 23 July 2024 may compute tax at 20% with indexation where that is lower. Specified mutual funds and market linked debentures are always short-term.

**Finance Act 2026: buyback.** Consideration received on a buyback of shares is now taxed as **capital gains** in the hands of all shareholders (it was taxed as deemed dividend from 1 October 2024 to 31 March 2026). The cost of the shares is deducted. Promoters bear an additional tax so that the effective rate is 22% for a promoter that is a domestic company and 30% for other promoters.

lesson.heading: Special cases of full value of consideration
lesson.body:
- **Stamp duty value of land or building** (corresponds to s.50C): if the stamp duty value exceeds the actual consideration by more than 10%, the stamp duty value is the full value of consideration.
- **Depreciable assets** (corresponds to s.50): gain on a block is always short-term, whatever the holding period.
- **Slump sale** (corresponds to s.50B): transfer of an undertaking for a lump sum. Gain = full value of consideration (the higher of actual consideration and fair market value under the rules) less **net worth**. Long-term if the undertaking was held for more than 36 months. No indexation.
- **Unquoted shares** (corresponds to s.50CA): FMV is the consideration if actual price is lower.
- **Conversion of firm assets on reconstitution** (corresponds to s.45(4) and s.9B): taxed in the hands of the firm.

Net worth in a slump sale:

| Particulars | Value taken |
| --- | --- |
| Depreciable assets | WDV as per tax records |
| Other assets | Book value (revaluation ignored) |
| Less: Liabilities of the undertaking | Book value |
| **Net worth** | **Aggregate** |

lesson.heading: Reinvestment exemptions
lesson.body:
| Exemption (1961 Act ref.) | Who | Asset sold | Invest in | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| s.54 | Individual, HUF | Long-term residential house | One residential house in India (two houses once in a lifetime if LTCG up to ₹2 crore) | Lower of LTCG and cost of new house; cap ₹10 crore |
| s.54EC | Any person | Long-term land or building | Specified bonds within 6 months | Up to ₹50 lakh; lock-in 5 years |
| s.54F | Individual, HUF | Any long-term asset other than a house | One residential house | LTCG x cost of new house / net consideration; cost capped at ₹10 crore |
| s.54B | Individual, HUF | Agricultural land used for 2 years | Agricultural land | Lower of gain and cost of new land |

Unutilised amounts must be deposited in the Capital Gains Account Scheme before the return due date.

**Worked example (s.54 and s.54EC).** Sale of a house (acquired 1 August 2024) on 10 September 2026 for ₹1,80,00,000; brokerage ₹1,80,000; cost ₹1,10,00,000; stamp duty value ₹1,95,00,000 (only 8.3% above consideration, so actual price is taken). LTCG = ₹68,20,000. New house bought for ₹50,00,000 and bonds for ₹8,00,000. Taxable LTCG = 68,20,000 - 50,00,000 - 8,00,000 = ₹10,20,000.

lesson.heading: Business reorganisation
lesson.body:
Transfers that are not regarded as transfer (corresponds to s.47) let groups restructure tax-neutrally:
- Transfer of capital assets in a scheme of **amalgamation** to an Indian amalgamated company; and the shareholder's exchange of shares in the amalgamating company for shares in the amalgamated company.
- Transfer in a **demerger** to an Indian resulting company, and issue of shares by the resulting company to shareholders of the demerged company.
- Conversion of a **private company or unlisted public company into an LLP** if turnover did not exceed ₹60 lakh and total assets did not exceed ₹5 crore in the three preceding years, shareholders become partners in the same proportion, and no shareholder receives other consideration.
- **Succession** of a sole proprietary concern or firm by a company, subject to conditions such as the proprietor holding at least 50% of voting power for 5 years.

The holding period and cost of the old shares carry over to the new shares. Carry forward of losses and unabsorbed depreciation on amalgamation (corresponds to s.72A) requires the amalgamating company to have been in business for 3 years, to hold at least 75% of the book value of fixed assets for 2 years, and the amalgamated company to hold 75% of those assets and continue the business for 5 years.

Common mistakes: applying s.54F when the assessee owns more than one other house; indexing a slump sale; forgetting that reorganisation exemptions fail if conditions are later breached (the exempt gain is then taxed in the year of breach).

keyPoints: STCG on STT-paid equity 20%; LTCG 12.5% above ₹1,25,000; other LTCG 12.5% without indexation.
Finance Act 2026: buyback consideration is taxed as capital gains; promoters face an effective 22% (corporate) or 30% (others).
Stamp duty value replaces consideration only if it exceeds it by more than 10% (corresponds to s.50C).
Slump sale gain = FVC less net worth (tax WDV for depreciable assets, book value for others); LTCA if held over 36 months.
s.54 and s.54F capped at ₹10 crore; s.54EC bonds up to ₹50 lakh within 6 months, 5-year lock-in.
Amalgamation, demerger and qualifying company-to-LLP conversions are not transfers; holding period carries over.

cases.title: Case: Orion Industries restructures
cases.body:
Orion Industries Ltd (an Indian company, in business since 2015) has two divisions. On 1 December 2026 it sells its **packaging division** to Delta Ltd for a lump sum of **₹12 crore**, without assigning values to individual assets. The division was set up in 2018. The fair market value of its assets under the valuation rules is ₹11 crore.

Balance sheet of the packaging division on the date of sale:

| Item | Book value (₹ crore) | Tax WDV (₹ crore) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plant and machinery (depreciable) | 3.50 | 3.00 |
| Land (revalued upward by ₹0.50 crore last year) | 2.50 | - |
| Inventory | 1.50 | - |
| Trade receivables | 1.00 | - |
| Trade payables and other liabilities | 2.50 | - |

Orion then plans to amalgamate its remaining business into its holding company, Polaris Ltd, an Indian company, in 2027.

questions.prompt: Compute the capital gain on the slump sale of the packaging division. Answer in ₹ lakh.
questions.explanation:
Net worth uses tax WDV for depreciable assets and book value without revaluation for others.

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Plant and machinery (tax WDV) | 3.00 |
| Land (book value 2.50 less revaluation 0.50) | 2.00 |
| Inventory | 1.50 |
| Trade receivables | 1.00 |
| Less: Liabilities | (2.50) |
| **Net worth** | **5.00** |

Full value of consideration = higher of ₹12 crore and FMV ₹11 crore = ₹12 crore. LTCG = 12.00 - 5.00 = ₹7 crore = ₹700 lakh. The division was held for more than 36 months, so the gain is long-term; no indexation.

questions.prompt: At what rate is the slump sale gain of Orion Industries taxed (before surcharge and cess)?
options: 12.5% without indexation
20% with indexation
Normal corporate rate as short-term gain
10% without indexation
questions.explanation: The undertaking was held for more than 36 months, so the gain is long-term and taxed at 12.5% without indexation (corresponds to s.112 and s.50B of the 1961 Act).

questions.prompt: On the later amalgamation into Polaris Ltd, the transfer of Orion's capital assets to Polaris will not be regarded as a transfer, because Polaris is an Indian company.
questions.explanation: A transfer of capital assets by an amalgamating company to an Indian amalgamated company in a scheme of amalgamation is not regarded as a transfer (corresponds to s.47(vi) of the 1961 Act).

questions.prompt: Mr Arjun, resident, sold a residential house on 10 September 2026. Compute his taxable long-term capital gain for tax year 2026-27 after exemptions. Answer in rupees.
questions.data:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Sale consideration | 1,80,00,000 |
| Stamp duty value | 1,95,00,000 |
| Brokerage paid | 1,80,000 |
| Cost of acquisition (house bought on 1 August 2024) | 1,10,00,000 |
| New residential house purchased in India on 15 December 2026 | 50,00,000 |
| Specified bonds bought on 20 January 2027 | 8,00,000 |
questions.explanation:
Stamp duty value is 108.3% of consideration (within the 10% tolerance), so actual consideration is used. The house was held for more than 24 months, so the gain is long-term; it was acquired after 23 July 2024, so no indexation option.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Sale consideration | 1,80,00,000 |
| Less: Brokerage | (1,80,000) |
| Less: Cost of acquisition | (1,10,00,000) |
| LTCG | 68,20,000 |
| Less: Exemption for new house (corresponds to s.54) | (50,00,000) |
| Less: Exemption for bonds within 6 months (corresponds to s.54EC) | (8,00,000) |
| **Taxable LTCG** | **10,20,000** |

questions.prompt: Ms Kavya, resident, has long-term capital gains of ₹3,40,000 on STT-paid listed equity shares in tax year 2026-27 and salary income well above the basic exemption limit. Compute the tax on these gains including 4% cess. Answer in rupees.
Mr Dev, resident, owning one residential house, sells unlisted shares held for 4 years. Compute the exemption available for investment in a new house (corresponds to s.54F). Answer in rupees.
questions.data:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Net consideration | 80,00,000 |
| Long-term capital gain | 40,00,000 |
| Cost of new residential house | 60,00,000 |
questions.explanation: Exemption = LTCG x cost of new house / net consideration = 40,00,000 x 60,00,000 / 80,00,000 = ₹30,00,000. He owns only one other house on the date of transfer, so the condition is met. Taxable LTCG = ₹10,00,000.

questions.prompt: Under the Finance Act 2026, how is the consideration received by a non-promoter resident shareholder on a buyback of shares by a listed company taxed?
options: As capital gains, after deducting the cost of the shares
As dividend under income from other sources, with the cost treated as a capital loss
Exempt in the shareholder's hands, as the company pays buyback tax
As business income at normal rates
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2026 moved buyback consideration back to capital gains for all shareholders. The deemed dividend approach (with the cost as a capital loss) applied only to buybacks from 1 October 2024 to 31 March 2026.

questions.prompt: A private company converts into an LLP. Which condition must be met for the conversion not to be a transfer?
options: Total sales did not exceed ₹60 lakh in any of the three preceding years
The company has been in existence for at least 10 years
Shareholders receive cash equal to their share capital
The LLP must be listed on a recognised stock exchange
questions.explanation: The conditions (corresponds to s.47(xiiib) of the 1961 Act) include turnover not exceeding ₹60 lakh and total assets not exceeding ₹5 crore in each of the three preceding years, all shareholders becoming partners in the same proportion, and no consideration other than profit share and capital contribution.

questions.prompt: Which of these transactions are not regarded as transfer for capital gains purposes? Select all that apply.
options: Transfer of assets by an amalgamating company to an Indian amalgamated company under a scheme
Issue of shares by an Indian resulting company to shareholders of the demerged company
Distribution of assets by a company to shareholders on liquidation
Sale of a business undertaking for a lump sum
Gift of a capital asset by an individual to a relative
questions.explanation: Amalgamation and demerger transfers and gifts by an individual are excluded from transfer. Distribution on liquidation is taxed in the shareholders' hands (corresponds to s.46), and a slump sale is a taxable transfer (corresponds to s.50B).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: in a slump sale the cost of acquisition of the undertaking is its ___ (two words).
questions.explanation: The cost of acquisition and improvement of the undertaking is deemed to be its net worth, computed using tax WDV for depreciable assets and book value (ignoring revaluation) for other assets.

questions.prompt: Land is sold for ₹90,00,000. Its stamp duty value is ₹1,00,00,000. What is the full value of consideration?
questions.explanation: 110% of ₹90,00,000 is ₹99,00,000. The stamp duty value of ₹1,00,00,000 exceeds it, so the stamp duty value is the full value of consideration.

questions.prompt: Explain, with a computation format, how capital gain is computed when a firm is reconstituted and a retiring partner receives a capital asset of the firm.
questions.answer:
**Provisions** (corresponds to s.45(4) and s.9B of the 1961 Act)

- When a partner receives money or a capital asset on reconstitution of the firm and the amount exceeds the partner's capital account balance, the excess is chargeable as capital gains in the hands of the **firm**.
- Separately, a capital asset given to a partner on dissolution or reconstitution is deemed a transfer by the firm at fair market value (s.9B treatment as business income or capital gains, as the asset may be).

**Format under s.45(4)**

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Money received + FMV of capital asset received by partner | xxx |
| Less: Balance in partner's capital account (ignoring revaluation and self-generated goodwill) | (xxx) |
| **Capital gain chargeable on firm** | **xxx** |

- The gain is attributed to remaining assets of the firm under the prescribed rules; it is short-term or long-term according to the asset to which it is attributed.
- In the hands of the partner, the receipt is exempt as share of the firm's assets.

questions.prompt: State the conditions for carry forward of the amalgamating company's accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation by the amalgamated company.
questions.answer:
(corresponds to s.72A of the 1961 Act)

- Available for amalgamation of a company owning an industrial undertaking, ship or hotel, or specified banks and others.
- Amalgamating company: engaged in the business for 3 or more years in which the loss arose, and held at least 75% of the book value of fixed assets continuously for 2 years before amalgamation.
- Amalgamated company: holds at least 75% of the book value of fixed assets acquired for 5 years, continues the business for at least 5 years, and fulfils the other prescribed conditions.
- The loss is deemed to be the loss of the amalgamated company for the year of amalgamation, giving a fresh period of carry forward.
- If conditions are breached later, the set-off already allowed is deemed income of the year of breach.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the exemptions for reinvestment in a residential house when the asset sold is a house and when it is any other long-term asset.
questions.answer:
- **House sold** (corresponds to s.54): exemption is the lower of LTCG and cost of the new house; no ownership restriction on other houses; option of two houses once if LTCG does not exceed ₹2 crore.
- **Other asset sold** (corresponds to s.54F): exemption is proportionate, LTCG x cost of new house / net consideration; the assessee must not own more than one residential house (other than the new one) on the date of transfer.
- Both: available to individuals and HUFs; purchase within 1 year before or 2 years after, or construction within 3 years; unutilised amount to be deposited in the Capital Gains Account Scheme by the return due date; cost counted only up to ₹10 crore.
- Both are withdrawn if the new house is sold within 3 years.

chapters.title: Taxation of Companies (MAT and Alternate Regimes), Firms, LLPs and AOPs
chapters.summary: Corporate tax rates and regime choice, MAT at 14% as a final tax after Finance Act 2026, and the special rules for firms, LLPs and AOPs.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Corporate rates and regimes
lesson.body:
| Company | Rate | Surcharge | Effective rate (with 4% cess) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Domestic, turnover up to ₹400 crore in tax year 2024-25 | 25% | 7% if income > ₹1 crore; 12% if > ₹10 crore | 25% to 29.12% |
| Other domestic | 30% | 7% / 12% | 31.2% to 34.944% |
| Concessional regime (corresponds to s.115BAA) | 22% | Flat 10% | 25.168% |
| New manufacturing company (corresponds to s.115BAB) | 15% | Flat 10% | 17.16% |
| Foreign company | 35% | 2% if > ₹1 crore; 5% if > ₹10 crore | 36.4% to 38.22% |

The concessional regime requires the company to forgo specified incentives: additional depreciation, deductions for specified businesses and scientific research above normal levels, and profit-linked deductions (other than a few, such as the deduction for new employment). Brought forward losses attributable to those incentives cannot be set off. The option, once exercised, cannot be withdrawn.

**Exam format for regime choice**: compute tax under the normal provisions (and MAT if higher), compute tax under the concessional regime after removing the forgone incentives, and recommend the lower outflow, noting the loss of MAT credit and incentives.

lesson.heading: Minimum alternate tax after Finance Act 2026
lesson.body:
MAT and the alternate minimum tax for non-corporate assessees are consolidated in **section 206** of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (corresponds to sections 115JB and 115JC of the 1961 Act). The Finance Act 2026 made three changes from 1 April 2026:

- **Rate**: MAT reduced from 15% to **14%** of book profit (plus surcharge and cess as applicable).
- **Final tax**: no new MAT credit arises for MAT paid from tax year 2026-27.
- **Old credit**: MAT credit accumulated up to 31 March 2026 can be carried forward up to the 15th year. A **domestic** company may set it off only if it moves to the new (concessional) regime, and only up to **one-fourth of its tax liability** in a year. A foreign company may set off credit to the extent normal tax exceeds MAT.

MAT does not apply to companies in the concessional regimes, and it has been extended to exclude all non-residents taxed on a presumptive basis.

Book profit starts from the net profit in the statement of profit and loss prepared under the Companies Act, adjusted only for the items specified (add income-tax provision, reserves, provision for unascertained liabilities, provision for diminution in value of assets, expenditure on exempt income; deduct exempt income credited, lower of brought forward loss and unabsorbed depreciation as per books, amounts withdrawn from reserves if added earlier).

lesson.heading: Firms, LLPs and AOPs
lesson.body:
**Firms and LLPs** are taxed at 30% (surcharge 12% if income exceeds ₹1 crore). Interest and remuneration to partners are deductible only within limits (corresponds to s.40(b)):
- Interest on capital: up to 12% simple interest per year, if authorised by the deed.
- Remuneration: only to working partners, authorised by the deed, within:

| Book profit | Maximum remuneration |
| --- | --- |
| First ₹6,00,000 or loss | Higher of ₹3,00,000 or 90% of book profit |
| Balance | 60% of book profit |

Book profit is net profit before deducting partner remuneration (after deducting allowable interest). In the partner's hands, the share of profit is exempt; interest and remuneration (to the extent allowed to the firm) are business income.

**LLPs and AMT**: an LLP or other non-corporate person claiming specified deductions (profit-linked deductions or deduction for specified business) pays alternate minimum tax of 18.5% of adjusted total income where regular tax is lower. AMT credit rules differ from the new MAT rules; check the ICAI material.

**AOP/BOI**: if members' shares are indeterminate, the AOP pays tax at the maximum marginal rate on its whole income. If shares are determinate and no member's income exceeds the basic exemption, slab rates apply; where any member is taxable at a higher rate, special rules apply. A member's share of AOP income is excluded from the member's tax on which the AOP has paid tax.

**Worked example.** Book profit ₹15,00,000; remuneration paid ₹12,00,000. Allowable = 90% of 6,00,000 + 60% of 9,00,000 = ₹10,80,000. Disallowed ₹1,20,000.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Applying the 7%/12% surcharge to a concessional regime company (the surcharge is a flat 10%).
- Computing MAT credit for tax year 2026-27 (no new credit arises after the Finance Act 2026).
- Allowing remuneration to a sleeping partner, or interest above 12%.
- Taking book profit after deducting remuneration in the s.40(b) computation.
- Forgetting the turnover test year for the 25% rate: it is turnover of the second preceding tax year.

keyPoints: Domestic company: 25% (turnover up to ₹400 crore) or 30%; concessional 22% + 10% surcharge = 25.168%; new manufacturing 15% = 17.16%.
Foreign company: 35% plus surcharge 2% or 5% and 4% cess.
MAT is in section 206 of the 2025 Act; 14% of book profit from tax year 2026-27 and a final tax.
Old MAT credit: domestic company sets off only under the new regime, capped at 25% of tax liability; carry forward to the 15th year.
Partner remuneration limit: higher of ₹3,00,000 or 90% on first ₹6,00,000 of book profit, 60% of the balance; interest up to 12%.
AOP with indeterminate shares pays tax at the maximum marginal rate.

cases.title: Case: Vardhan Components Pvt Ltd chooses a regime
cases.body:
Vardhan Components Pvt Ltd is a domestic company with turnover of ₹600 crore in tax year 2024-25. For tax year 2026-27:

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Total income under normal provisions (after additional depreciation of ₹2 crore) | 8.00 |
| Total income if the concessional regime is opted (additional depreciation not allowed) | 10.00 |
| Book profit for MAT | 12.00 |

The company has no brought forward losses and no MAT credit. Assume no other incentive is lost by opting for the concessional regime.

questions.prompt: Compute the tax liability of Vardhan Components under the normal provisions (ignore MAT). Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
Turnover of ₹600 crore exceeds ₹400 crore, so the rate is 30%. Income ₹8 crore is between ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore, so surcharge is 7%.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Tax at 30% on 8,00,00,000 | 2,40,00,000 |
| Surcharge 7% | 16,80,000 |
| | 2,56,80,000 |
| Cess 4% | 10,27,200 |
| **Tax** | **2,67,07,200** |

questions.prompt: Compute the MAT liability of Vardhan Components at the rate applicable after the Finance Act 2026. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
Book profit ₹12 crore exceeds ₹10 crore, so surcharge is 12%.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| MAT at 14% on 12,00,00,000 | 1,68,00,000 |
| Surcharge 12% | 20,16,000 |
| | 1,88,16,000 |
| Cess 4% | 7,52,640 |
| **MAT** | **1,95,68,640** |

Normal tax (₹2,67,07,200) is higher, so MAT does not apply under the normal regime.

questions.prompt: Compute the tax liability of Vardhan Components if it opts for the concessional 22% regime. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Tax at 22% on 10,00,00,000 | 2,20,00,000 |
| Surcharge flat 10% | 22,00,000 |
| | 2,42,00,000 |
| Cess 4% | 9,68,000 |
| **Tax** | **2,51,68,000** |

The concessional regime saves ₹15,39,200 compared with the normal provisions (2,67,07,200 - 2,51,68,000), even after losing additional depreciation, and MAT does not apply.

questions.prompt: If Vardhan Components had brought forward MAT credit of ₹40 lakh from years before 1 April 2026, how could it use the credit under the Finance Act 2026 rules?
options: Only after moving to the new regime, up to one-fourth of its tax liability each year
Against normal tax to the extent normal tax exceeds MAT, without any cap
It lapses on 1 April 2026
It is refunded in cash in tax year 2026-27
questions.explanation: As reported in the Finance Act 2026 changes, a domestic company can set off MAT credit accumulated up to 31 March 2026 only when it is in the new regime, capped at 25% of the tax liability for the year. The unlimited set-off of normal tax over MAT now applies only to foreign companies.

questions.prompt: Compute the remuneration to working partners allowable as a deduction to a firm whose book profit for tax year 2026-27 is ₹15,00,000 (the deed authorises remuneration of ₹12,00,000). Answer in rupees.

A domestic company (turnover ₹150 crore in tax year 2024-25, normal regime) has total income of ₹2 crore and book profit of ₹5 crore for tax year 2026-27. Compute its final tax liability. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Normal (₹) | MAT (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base | 25% x 2,00,00,000 = 50,00,000 | 14% x 5,00,00,000 = 70,00,000 |
| Surcharge 7% | 3,50,000 | 4,90,000 |
| Cess 4% | 2,14,000 | 2,99,600 |
| Total | 55,64,000 | 77,89,600 |

MAT is higher, so the liability is **₹77,89,600**. Under the Finance Act 2026 no MAT credit arises for the excess.

questions.prompt: Which provision of the Income-tax Act, 2025 contains both minimum alternate tax for companies and alternate minimum tax for other persons?
options: Section 206
Section 58
Section 165
Section 202
questions.explanation: Section 206 consolidates the MAT and AMT provisions (sections 115JB and 115JC of the 1961 Act). Section 58 is presumptive taxation, section 165 is arm's length price and section 202 is the individual new regime.

questions.prompt: A company that has opted for the 22% concessional regime must still compare its tax with MAT at 14% of book profit.
questions.explanation: MAT does not apply to companies in the concessional regimes (corresponds to s.115BAA and s.115BAB of the 1961 Act).

questions.prompt: Which adjustments are made to net profit in computing book profit for MAT? Select all that apply.
options: Add back provision for income-tax
Add back provision for diminution in value of assets
Deduct depreciation at income-tax rates
Add back amounts transferred to reserves
Deduct lower of brought forward loss and unabsorbed depreciation as per books
questions.explanation: Book profit uses depreciation as per books, not tax depreciation. Income-tax, reserves and provision for diminution are added back; the lower of book loss and book unabsorbed depreciation is deducted.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the maximum rate of interest on partners' capital allowed as a deduction to a firm is ___% simple interest per year.
questions.explanation: Interest above 12% simple interest per year is disallowed (corresponds to s.40(b)(iv) of the 1961 Act).

questions.prompt: Members of an AOP have not specified their shares in its income. At what rate is the AOP taxed?
options: Maximum marginal rate on the whole income
Slab rates applicable to individuals
Flat 30% without surcharge
25% like a small company
questions.explanation: Where individual shares are indeterminate or unknown, the AOP is taxed at the maximum marginal rate on its total income.

questions.prompt: Shree Associates, a firm of three working partners, shows net profit of ₹18,00,000 for tax year 2026-27 after debiting interest on capital at 15% (₹3,00,000) and partner remuneration of ₹9,00,000. All payments are authorised by the deed. Compute the total income of the firm and its tax.
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Interest**

Interest allowed at 12%: 3,00,000 x 12/15 = ₹2,40,000. Disallowed ₹60,000.

**Step 2: Book profit**

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Net profit | 18,00,000 |
| Add: Remuneration debited | 9,00,000 |
| Add: Excess interest | 60,000 |
| **Book profit** | **27,60,000** |

**Step 3: Allowable remuneration**

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| 90% of first 6,00,000 | 5,40,000 |
| 60% of balance 21,60,000 | 12,96,000 |
| Limit | 18,36,000 |
| Actual paid | 9,00,000 |
| **Allowed (lower)** | **9,00,000** |

**Step 4: Total income and tax**

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Book profit | 27,60,000 |
| Less: Remuneration allowed | (9,00,000) |
| **Total income** | **18,60,000** |
| Tax at 30% | 5,58,000 |
| Cess 4% | 22,320 |
| **Tax liability** | **5,80,320** |

No surcharge as income does not exceed ₹1 crore.

questions.prompt: Explain the changes made to MAT by the Finance Act 2026 and their effect on a company's choice between the normal and concessional regimes.
questions.answer:
- MAT rate reduced from 15% to 14% of book profit from 1 April 2026 (section 206 of the 2025 Act, corresponds to s.115JB).
- MAT becomes a final tax: no new credit accumulates for MAT paid from tax year 2026-27.
- Credit accumulated up to 31 March 2026 can be carried forward to the 15th year; a domestic company can use it only after moving to the new (concessional) regime, limited to one-fourth of tax liability each year. Foreign companies can set off credit to the extent normal tax exceeds MAT.
- Effect: staying in the normal regime only to preserve MAT credit no longer works; companies with large credits have a reason to switch, subject to the cap and the loss of incentives.
- MAT exemption extended to all non-residents taxed on a presumptive basis.

questions.prompt: How are a partner's share of profit, interest and remuneration from a firm taxed in the partner's hands?
questions.answer:
- Share of profit from a firm assessed as a firm is exempt in the partner's hands (corresponds to s.10(2A)).
- Interest on capital and remuneration are taxed as profits and gains of business or profession, but only to the extent allowed as a deduction to the firm (corresponds to s.28(v)). Any disallowed excess is not taxed in the partner's hands.
- Expenses incurred by the partner to earn the interest or remuneration (for example interest on money borrowed to contribute capital) are deductible.
- The same treatment applies to partners of an LLP.

chapters.title: Taxation of Trusts and Charitable Institutions
chapters.summary: Registration, the 85% application rule, accumulation, anonymous donations, commercial receipts and accreted income for not-for-profit organisations.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Where the provisions sit
lesson.body:
The Income-tax Act, 2025 groups the rules for registered not-for-profit organisations (NPOs) in a separate part, broadly sections 332 to 355. Registration is in section 332 (corresponds to sections 12A and 12AB of the 1961 Act), and the provisions on income, application and violations correspond to sections 11, 12 and 13 of the 1961 Act. Funds and institutions earlier approved under section 10(23C) are listed in Schedule VII; the Finance Act 2026 provides that funds covered by entries 10 to 16 of that Schedule no longer need separate NPO registration.

Because exact sub-section references are still settling in study material, this chapter names the provision and gives the 1961 Act section.

Registration framework:
- Provisional registration for 3 years for a new trust, from the date of application.
- Regular registration for 5 years, renewable (a longer period applies to smaller trusts; verify the current rule).
- Registration can be cancelled for **specified violations**, such as applying income other than for objects, carrying on business in violation of conditions, or benefit to specified persons.

lesson.heading: Income, application and accumulation
lesson.body:
A registered trust's income from property held for charitable or religious purposes is exempt to the extent it is **applied** in India for its objects. The key tests:

| Rule | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Application | At least 85% of income must be applied in the year |
| Free accumulation | 15% of income may be set apart without conditions |
| Deemed application | If income is not received, or for other reasons, it may be applied in the next year by option |
| Specified accumulation | Shortfall may be accumulated for up to 5 years for a stated purpose, by filing the prescribed form before the return due date, and investing in specified modes |
| Corpus donations | Exempt if received with a specific direction to form part of corpus and invested in specified modes |
| Application from corpus or loan | Not application when spent; allowed when the corpus or loan is reinvested or repaid |
| Donations to other trusts | Only 85% of such donation counts as application; corpus donations to other trusts are not application |
| Depreciation | Not allowed on an asset whose cost was claimed as application |

**Worked example.** Voluntary contributions (non-corpus) ₹50,00,000 and rent ₹30,00,000: income ₹80,00,000. Applied ₹60,00,000. Free accumulation 15% = ₹12,00,000. Taxable = 80,00,000 - 60,00,000 - 12,00,000 = ₹8,00,000 (unless specifically accumulated).

lesson.heading: Special charges and denial of exemption
lesson.body:
- **Anonymous donations** (corresponds to s.115BBC): taxed at 30% to the extent they exceed the higher of 5% of total donations or ₹1,00,000. Wholly religious trusts are outside this rule; partly religious trusts are taxed on anonymous donations for non-religious purposes.
- **Business activity**: a trust for advancement of any other object of general public utility may carry on trade or commerce only if receipts from such activity do not exceed **20%** of total receipts of the year (corresponds to the proviso to s.2(15)). If exceeded, it is not charitable for that year.
- **Benefit to specified persons** (author, trustees, substantial contributors and their relatives): income used for their benefit loses exemption (corresponds to s.13(1)(c)); the tax on such income is at the maximum marginal rate.
- **Investments outside specified modes**: income from them is not exempt.
- **Accreted income** (corresponds to s.115TD): if the trust converts into a non-charitable form, merges with a non-charitable entity (or a merger fails the conditions), or its registration is cancelled, the fair market value of assets less liabilities is taxed at the maximum marginal rate. The Finance Act 2026 adds a merger provision for NPOs with the same or similar objects, modelled on s.12AC.

**Compliance**: audit of accounts where total income before exemption exceeds the basic exemption limit; the Finance Act 2026 moves the return due date for non-audit trusts to 31 August.

lesson.heading: Exam approach and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Format for income of a trust:

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Income from property (gross receipts less revenue outgoings) | xxx |
| Voluntary contributions (other than corpus) | xxx |
| **Income** | **xxx** |
| Less: Applied for objects (revenue and capital) | (xxx) |
| Less: 15% free accumulation | (xxx) |
| Less: Specified accumulation (if form filed) | (xxx) |
| **Taxable income** | **xxx** |

Common mistakes: including corpus donations in income; allowing depreciation on assets already treated as application; applying the 85% test on receipts after deducting accumulation; treating the 20% commercial receipts limit as profit rather than receipts.

keyPoints: NPO provisions sit in sections 332 to 355 of the 2025 Act (registration: section 332; corresponds to ss.11, 12, 12A, 12AB, 13).
Apply at least 85% of income; 15% may be accumulated freely; shortfall may be accumulated for up to 5 years by filing the form.
Corpus donations are exempt if invested in specified modes; spending from corpus counts as application only on reinvestment.
Anonymous donations above the higher of 5% of total donations or ₹1,00,000 are taxed at 30%.
General public utility trusts lose charitable status if business receipts exceed 20% of total receipts.
Accreted income on conversion, failed merger or cancellation is taxed at the maximum marginal rate.

cases.title: Case: Seva Sadan Trust
cases.body:
Seva Sadan Trust is registered as a charitable NPO running a free clinic. For tax year 2026-27:

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Rent from property held under trust | 30,00,000 |
| Voluntary contributions (no direction) | 50,00,000 |
| Corpus donations with a specific direction (invested in a bank FD) | 20,00,000 |
| Expenses on running the clinic | 45,00,000 |
| Purchase of medical equipment | 15,00,000 |
| Salary to the founder's son as clinic administrator at twice the market rate | 6,00,000 (market rate ₹3,00,000) |

The trust has not filed any form for specified accumulation. The salary of ₹6,00,000 is included in the clinic expenses of ₹45,00,000.

questions.prompt: What is the 'income' of Seva Sadan Trust against which the 85% application test is applied?
questions.explanation: Income = rent ₹30,00,000 + non-corpus voluntary contributions ₹50,00,000 = ₹80,00,000. Corpus donations with a specific direction and invested in specified modes are excluded.

questions.prompt: Ignoring the excess salary issue, compute the income of Seva Sadan Trust chargeable to tax for tax year 2026-27 under the application rules. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Income | 80,00,000 |
| Less: Applied - clinic expenses | (45,00,000) |
| Less: Applied - medical equipment | (15,00,000) |
| Less: Free accumulation 15% of 80,00,000 | (12,00,000) |
| **Taxable** | **8,00,000** |

No form for specified accumulation was filed, so the shortfall is taxable.

questions.prompt: The excess salary of ₹3,00,000 paid to the founder's son is a benefit to a specified person, and income to that extent loses exemption.
questions.explanation: Payment to a relative of the author in excess of what is reasonable for services is a use of income for the benefit of a specified person (corresponds to s.13(1)(c) and 13(2)(c) of the 1961 Act). The excess loses exemption and is taxed at the maximum marginal rate; it can also be a specified violation.

questions.prompt: Seva Sadan Trust claims depreciation of ₹2,25,000 on the medical equipment in the same year. How is this treated?
options: Not allowed, because the cost was already claimed as application
Allowed as application in addition to the cost
Allowed only at half rate
Allowed if the trust accumulates 15%
questions.explanation: Depreciation on an asset whose cost has been claimed as application is not allowed, to prevent a double deduction.

questions.prompt: A charitable (not religious) trust receives total donations of ₹60,00,000 in tax year 2026-27, including anonymous donations of ₹5,00,000. Compute the tax on anonymous donations including 4% cess. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Anonymous donations | 5,00,000 |
| Less: Higher of 5% of 60,00,000 (3,00,000) and 1,00,000 | (3,00,000) |
| Taxable anonymous donations | 2,00,000 |
| Tax at 30% | 60,000 |
| Cess 4% | 2,400 |
| **Total** | **62,400** |

questions.prompt: A trust for advancement of general public utility has total receipts of ₹2 crore, of which ₹45 lakh is from a commercial activity. Compute commercial receipts as a percentage of total receipts. Answer as a % to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: 45,00,000 / 2,00,00,000 x 100 = 22.50%. This exceeds the 20% limit, so the activity is not a charitable purpose for that year and the exemption is lost for the year.

questions.prompt: A trust spends ₹10,00,000 out of its corpus fund on a school building in tax year 2026-27. When is this treated as application of income?
options: When the amount is reinvested or deposited back into the corpus
In tax year 2026-27, when spent
Never
Only if the trust files the specified accumulation form
questions.explanation: Application out of corpus is not application in the year of spending. It is allowed as application when the trust reinvests or deposits back an equal amount into the corpus in specified modes, within the time allowed.

questions.prompt: Which events can attract tax on accreted income of a registered trust? Select all that apply.
options: Conversion into a form not eligible for registration
Merger with an entity with dissimilar objects or not registered
Cancellation of registration
Applying 90% of income in a year
Failure to apply for renewal of registration within time
questions.explanation: Accreted income is taxed on conversion, merger that fails conditions, cancellation and failure to renew registration within the time allowed (corresponds to s.115TD). Applying more than 85% is compliance, not a trigger.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a registered trust may accumulate ___% of its income without any conditions.
questions.explanation: Up to 15% of income may be set apart freely; the remaining 85% must be applied or specifically accumulated.

questions.prompt: Which section of the Income-tax Act, 2025 deals with registration of NPOs (corresponds to sections 12A and 12AB of the 1961 Act)?
options: Section 332
Section 206
Section 58
Section 393
questions.explanation: Registration of NPOs is in section 332 of the 2025 Act. Section 206 is MAT, section 58 is presumptive taxation, section 393 is TDS.

questions.prompt: A donation by one registered trust to another registered trust towards its corpus is treated as application of income by the donor trust.
questions.explanation: Corpus donations to another trust are not treated as application. Non-corpus donations to another registered trust count as application only to the extent of 85%.

questions.prompt: Gyan Jyoti Trust (registered, education) has income of ₹1,20,00,000 for tax year 2026-27 and applies ₹80,00,000. It wants to build a new hostel over three years. Advise it on avoiding tax on the shortfall and compute the minimum amount to be specifically accumulated.
questions.answer:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Income | 1,20,00,000 |
| Required application 85% | 1,02,00,000 |
| Actual application | 80,00,000 |
| **Shortfall to be specifically accumulated** | **22,00,000** |

Advice:
- Pass a resolution stating the purpose (hostel construction) and the period (not more than 5 years).
- File the prescribed form for accumulation before the due date of the return and file the return by the due date.
- Invest the accumulated ₹22,00,000 in specified modes (for example scheduled bank deposits).
- Apply the amount for the stated purpose within 5 years; any unapplied amount, or amount used for other purposes, is taxed in the year of failure.
- The 15% (₹18,00,000) is free accumulation and needs no conditions.

questions.prompt: Explain the conditions under which an educational or medical trust's income from property held under trust is exempt.
questions.answer:
- The trust must be registered under section 332 of the 2025 Act (corresponds to s.12AB) and file its return and audit report on time.
- At least 85% of income must be applied in India for its objects during the year; the balance may be accumulated (15% freely, more with the prescribed form for up to 5 years).
- Funds must be invested in specified modes (corresponds to s.11(5)).
- No part of income or property may be used for the benefit of specified persons (corresponds to s.13).
- For general public utility trusts, business receipts must not exceed 20% of total receipts.
- Anonymous donations above the exempt limit are taxed at 30%.
- Corpus donations with a specific direction are exempt if invested in specified modes.

questions.prompt: What is accreted income and how is it computed and taxed?
questions.answer:
- Accreted income is the fair market value of the total assets of a registered trust minus its total liabilities, computed by the prescribed method on the specified date (corresponds to s.115TD).
- Assets acquired out of agricultural income and assets whose income was not exempt are excluded.
- It is charged at the maximum marginal rate in addition to normal income tax, on conversion into a non-charitable form, merger failing the conditions, cancellation of registration, failure to apply for registration, or transfer of assets on dissolution to non-charitable entities.
- The trust and the trustees are liable; interest applies if not paid within the time allowed.
- The Finance Act 2026 aligns these rules with the new NPO merger provision.

chapters.title: TDS, TCS, Advance Tax, Interest and Fees
chapters.summary: The consolidated TDS and TCS tables of the 2025 Act, Finance Act 2026 rate changes, advance tax instalments and interest for defaults.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Structure under the 2025 Act
lesson.body:
The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the long list of TDS sections (192 to 196D of the 1961 Act) with tables in **section 393** and puts TCS in **section 394**. Definitions used in these sections (such as "work") are in section 402; the Finance Act 2026 amended section 402(47) so that **supply of manpower** is treated as work, attracting contractor rates of 1% or 2% instead of the professional rate.

Key rates and thresholds for residents (named by the 1961 Act section they correspond to):

| Payment (1961 ref.) | Threshold | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contractor (194C) | ₹30,000 single, ₹1,00,000 aggregate | 1% individual/HUF, 2% others |
| Professional fees (194J) | ₹50,000 per year | 10% |
| Technical services, call centre (194J) | ₹50,000 per year | 2% |
| Rent: land, building, furniture (194-I) | ₹50,000 per month or part | 10% |
| Rent: plant and machinery (194-I) | ₹50,000 per month or part | 2% |
| Commission (194H) | ₹20,000 per year | 2% |
| Purchase of goods (194Q) | Above ₹50 lakh, buyer turnover > ₹10 crore | 0.1% |
| Non-residents (195) | No threshold | Rates in force or DTAA rate |

Without PAN, tax is deducted at the higher of the normal rate and 20% (corresponds to s.206AA). The higher rate for non-filers (old s.206AB) was omitted from 1 April 2025.

lesson.heading: TCS changes by the Finance Act 2026
lesson.body:
| Item | Before 1 April 2026 | From 1 April 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overseas tour programme package | 5% up to ₹10 lakh, 20% above | **2% with no threshold** |
| LRS remittance for education or medical treatment | 5% above ₹10 lakh | **2%** above ₹10 lakh |
| LRS remittance for other purposes | 20% above ₹10 lakh | No change |
| Alcoholic liquor, scrap, coal, lignite, iron ore | 1% | **2%** |
| Tendu leaves | 5% | **2%** |

Late payment of TDS or TCS carries interest: 1% per month (or part) from the date tax was deductible to the date deducted, and 1.5% per month from the date deducted to the date paid. A fee of ₹200 per day applies for late filing of TDS/TCS statements, capped at the tax deductible (corresponds to s.234E). The Finance Act 2026 also allows Form 15G/15H to be filed once with a depository and shared with payers.

lesson.heading: Advance tax and interest
lesson.body:
Advance tax is payable when tax liability after TDS/TCS is ₹10,000 or more. A resident senior citizen with no business income is exempt.

| Due date | Cumulative % (non-presumptive) |
| --- | --- |
| 15 June | 15% |
| 15 September | 45% |
| 15 December | 75% |
| 15 March | 100% |

Presumptive assessees under section 58 pay 100% by 15 March.

**Interest for default in payment of advance tax** (corresponds to s.234B): if advance tax paid is less than 90% of assessed tax, 1% per month or part on the shortfall, from 1 April following the tax year to the date of determination of income (or payment of self-assessment tax).

**Interest for deferment** (corresponds to s.234C): 1% per month on the shortfall for 3 months for each of the first three instalments, and 1 month for the last. No interest for the June instalment if 12% was paid, and for September if 36% was paid. Shortfall is rounded down to the nearest ₹100.

**Interest for late return** (corresponds to s.234A): 1% per month or part on tax unpaid, from the day after the due date to the date of filing.

**Worked example (234C).** Tax due ₹4,00,000; paid cumulatively ₹30,000, ₹1,20,000, ₹2,50,000 and ₹4,00,000.

| Instalment | Required | Paid | Shortfall | Interest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| June (15%) | 60,000 | 30,000 (below 12%) | 30,000 | 900 |
| September (45%) | 1,80,000 | 1,20,000 (below 36%) | 60,000 | 1,800 |
| December (75%) | 3,00,000 | 2,50,000 | 50,000 | 1,500 |
| March (100%) | 4,00,000 | 4,00,000 | Nil | Nil |
| **Total** | | | | **4,200** |

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Computing rent TDS threshold on annual rent; it is ₹50,000 per month or part of a month.
- Treating manpower supply as professional services after the Finance Act 2026.
- Applying the 12%/36% safe limits to the December instalment (there is no safe limit for December).
- Counting interest under s.201(1A) from the date of payment instead of the date the tax was deductible.
- Forgetting that interest on late deduction and on late payment are two separate periods with different rates.

keyPoints: TDS is in the tables of section 393 and TCS in section 394 of the 2025 Act; definitions in section 402.
Finance Act 2026: manpower supply is 'work' (contractor TDS 1%/2%); overseas tour package TCS 2% flat; LRS education/medical 2%; liquor, scrap and minerals 2%.
Rent TDS: ₹50,000 per month threshold; 10% building, 2% plant.
Advance tax: 15/45/75/100% by 15 June, September, December, March; section 58 assessees 100% by 15 March.
Interest: 1% per month for 234A, 234B, 234C; TDS default 1% (not deducted) and 1.5% (not paid).
Late statement fee ₹200 per day, capped at TDS amount.

cases.title: Case: Prakash Industries Ltd
cases.body:
Prakash Industries Ltd (resident, turnover ₹80 crore) made these payments to residents in tax year 2026-27:

| Payment | Amount | Facts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rent for office building | ₹70,000 per month for 12 months | Landlord is an individual with PAN |
| Supply of security guards by an agency (a firm) | ₹12,00,000 for the year | Invoices of ₹1,00,000 per month |
| Legal fees to an advocate | ₹4,00,000 | Advocate has PAN |
| TDS of ₹50,000 on a payment | Deductible on 10 June 2026 | Deducted on 25 August 2026 and paid on 15 October 2026 |

questions.prompt: Compute TDS on the office rent paid by Prakash Industries for the year. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Rent exceeds ₹50,000 per month, so TDS applies at 10% for land and building: 70,000 x 12 x 10% = ₹84,000.

questions.prompt: At what rate should Prakash Industries deduct tax on the payment to the security agency after the Finance Act 2026?
options: 2%, as payment to a contractor other than an individual or HUF
10%, as fees for professional services
1%, as payment to an individual contractor
No TDS, as it is a service contract
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2026 treats supply of manpower as 'work' under section 402(47), so contractor rates apply. The agency is a firm, so the rate is 2%.

questions.prompt: Compute interest payable by Prakash Industries for the delay in deducting and paying the TDS of ₹50,000. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Period | Months (part = full) | Rate | Interest (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 June to 25 August (not deducted) | 3 | 1% | 1,500 |
| 25 August to 15 October (deducted, not paid) | 2 | 1.5% | 1,500 |
| **Total** | | | **3,000** |

questions.prompt: Prakash Industries must deduct tax at 10% on the legal fees of ₹4,00,000 paid to the advocate.
questions.explanation: Legal fees are fees for professional services; the payment exceeds the ₹50,000 threshold, so TDS at 10% applies (corresponds to s.194J).

questions.prompt: Compute interest for deferment of advance tax (corresponds to s.234C) for tax year 2026-27. Answer in rupees.
questions.data: Tax on returned income less TDS: ₹4,00,000. Cumulative advance tax paid: by 15 June ₹30,000; by 15 September ₹1,20,000; by 15 December ₹2,50,000; by 15 March ₹4,00,000.

questions.prompt: Assessed tax (after TDS) for tax year 2026-27 is ₹5,00,000. Advance tax paid is ₹4,00,000. The balance is paid as self-assessment tax on 31 July 2027 with the return. Compute interest for default in payment of advance tax (corresponds to s.234B). Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Advance tax paid (₹4,00,000) is 80% of assessed tax, below 90%, so interest applies. Shortfall ₹1,00,000 x 1% x 4 months (April to July 2027) = ₹4,000.

questions.prompt: What is the TCS rate on sale of an overseas tour programme package of ₹6,00,000 to a resident individual in tax year 2026-27?
options: Nil, as it is below ₹10 lakh
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2026 replaced the 5%/20% structure with a flat 2% on overseas tour packages, without any threshold.

questions.prompt: Which provision of the Income-tax Act, 2025 contains the TCS table?
options: Section 394
Section 393
Section 263
Section 159
questions.explanation: TCS is in section 394; TDS is in section 393; section 263 deals with return of income; section 159 is double taxation relief.

questions.prompt: Which persons pay advance tax in a single instalment by 15 March, or not at all? Select all that apply.
options: A resident individual opting for presumptive business income under section 58
A resident senior citizen (age 65) with only pension and interest income (not liable to advance tax)
A company with tax liability of ₹5 crore
A professional opting for presumptive income at 50% of receipts
A salaried employee with ₹50,000 tax due after TDS
questions.explanation: Presumptive business and profession assessees pay the whole advance tax by 15 March. A resident senior citizen without business income is not liable. Companies and the salaried employee follow the four-instalment schedule.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the fee for late filing of a TDS statement is ₹___ per day of default.
questions.explanation: ₹200 per day, subject to a maximum of the TDS amount (corresponds to s.234E).

questions.prompt: A payee resident in India does not furnish PAN. The normal TDS rate is 10%. What rate applies?
questions.explanation: Tax is deducted at the higher of the normal rate and 20% where PAN is not furnished (corresponds to s.206AA).

questions.prompt: Mrs Rao (resident, age 45, business income, new regime) estimates tax of ₹3,60,000 for tax year 2026-27. TDS of ₹60,000 is expected. Prepare her advance tax schedule, and compute interest under s.234C if she pays nothing until 15 December and then pays ₹3,00,000 on 15 December.
questions.answer:
Advance tax liability = 3,60,000 - 60,000 = ₹3,00,000.

**Schedule**

| Due date | Cumulative % | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 June 2026 | 15% | 45,000 |
| 15 September 2026 | 45% | 1,35,000 |
| 15 December 2026 | 75% | 2,25,000 |
| 15 March 2027 | 100% | 3,00,000 |

**Interest (corresponds to s.234C)**

| Instalment | Shortfall (₹) | Months | Interest (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| June | 45,000 | 3 | 1,350 |
| September | 1,35,000 | 3 | 4,050 |
| December | Nil (paid 3,00,000) | - | Nil |
| March | Nil | - | Nil |
| **Total** | | | **5,400** |

No interest under s.234B as 100% is paid before 31 March.

questions.prompt: What are the consequences of failure to deduct or pay TDS?
questions.answer:
- The payer is an assessee in default for the tax not deducted or not paid (corresponds to s.201(1)); no default if the payee has included the income in a return and paid tax, with an accountant's certificate.
- Interest at 1% per month from the date deductible to the date deducted, and 1.5% per month from the date deducted to the date paid (s.201(1A)).
- Disallowance in computing business income: 30% for resident payees, 100% for non-resident payees, until TDS is paid.
- Penalty equal to the tax not deducted (corresponds to s.271C), now rationalised by the Finance Act 2026 with the penalty imposed in the common order.
- Prosecution for failure to pay tax deducted, subject to the Finance Act 2026 decriminalisation of certain defaults (for example TDS on payments in kind).
- Fee of ₹200 per day for late statements.

questions.prompt: Explain the TCS changes on foreign remittances and overseas tour packages made by the Finance Act 2026.
questions.answer:
- Overseas tour programme packages: flat 2% from the first rupee, replacing 5% up to ₹10 lakh and 20% above.
- LRS remittances for education and medical treatment: 2% on amounts above ₹10 lakh (earlier 5%).
- Other LRS remittances: 20% above ₹10 lakh, unchanged.
- TCS on liquor, scrap and specified minerals raised from 1% to 2%; tendu leaves reduced from 5% to 2%.
- No TCS where the buyer is liable to deduct TDS on the same transaction.
- TCS is credited against the buyer's tax liability; it is not an additional tax.
