chapters.title: Assessment, Appeals, Revision, Penalties and Prosecution
chapters.summary: Scrutiny and reassessment, appeals and revision, and the penalty and prosecution regime as rationalised by the Finance Act 2026.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Assessment and reassessment
lesson.body:
Return filing is in section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (corresponds to s.139 of the 1961 Act). The Finance Act 2026 set the due dates as 31 July for individuals filing the simplest returns, 31 August for non-audit business cases and trusts, and 31 October (30 November for transfer pricing cases) for audit cases. A revised return can be filed up to 31 March after the end of the tax year, (earlier 31 December); a revision after the old window attracts a fee of ₹1,000 where total income is up to ₹5 lakh and ₹5,000 in other cases.

Types of assessment (named by the corresponding 1961 Act section; check 2025 Act numbering in study material):
- **Summary processing** (s.143(1)): arithmetical errors, incorrect claims apparent from the return, disallowance of items in the audit report.
- **Scrutiny** (s.143(3)): notice within 3 months from the end of the financial year in which the return is filed; conducted in faceless mode.
- **Best judgment** (s.144): on failure to file a return or comply with notices.
- **Income escaping assessment** (s.147 to 151): an inquiry and show-cause stage precedes the notice. Notice may be issued up to 3 years from the end of the relevant year, or up to 5 years if escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more, with approval of the specified authority.
- **Search assessments**: the Finance Act 2026 extends the time limit for specified persons to 18 months from the initiation of search.

**Updated return**: may be filed within 48 months from the end of the relevant year by paying additional tax of 25%, 50%, 60% or 70% of tax and interest (within 12, 24, 36 or 48 months). The Finance Act 2026 allows an updated return even after reassessment proceedings start, at a further 10% additional tax, and grants no penalty on the additional income disclosed.

lesson.heading: Appeals and revision
lesson.body:
| Forum | Against | Time limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Joint Commissioner (Appeals) or Commissioner (Appeals) | Assessment and penalty orders | 30 days from service of order |
| Income Tax Appellate Tribunal | Order of CIT(A), DRP-directed orders, revision orders | 2 months from receipt of order |
| High Court | Substantial question of law from ITAT orders | 120 days |
| Supreme Court | High Court judgment (certified fit) | As per the Supreme Court rules |

**Pre-deposit for stay**: the Finance Act 2026 announcement reduces the pre-deposit for stay of demand pending first appeal from 20% to **10%**, computed on core tax demand only, and interest on penalty is held in abeyance during the first appeal.

**Revision**:
- By the Principal Commissioner when an order is **erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of revenue** (corresponds to s.263): within 2 years from the end of the financial year of the order; the assessee must be heard.
- On the assessee's application or suo motu, in favour of the assessee (corresponds to s.264): application within 1 year; cannot be made where an appeal is pending or the time for appeal has not expired and the right is not waived.

**Dispute Resolution Panel** is available to eligible assessees (foreign companies and transfer pricing cases) against draft orders.

lesson.heading: Penalties after the Finance Act 2026
lesson.body:
**Under-reporting and misreporting of income** (corresponds to s.270A):

| Situation | Penalty |
| --- | --- |
| Under-reported income | 50% of tax payable on under-reported income |
| Under-reported income in consequence of misreporting (misrepresentation, unrecorded investments, false entries, etc.) | 200% of such tax |

Tax payable on under-reported income = tax on (returned income + under-reported income) minus tax on returned income.

Finance Act 2026 changes:
- **One common order**: assessment and penalty are decided together in a single order after hearing.
- **Immunity** from penalty and prosecution (corresponds to s.270AA), earlier only for under-reporting, is extended to misreporting on payment of tax plus an amount equal to 100% of tax (sections 478 and 479 of the 2025 Act).
- **Special income** (cash credits, unexplained investments, money, expenditure; corresponds to s.115BBE): rate reduced from 60% to **30%** (section 195 of the 2025 Act); the separate 10% penalty is merged into the 200% misreporting penalty.
- **Technical defaults** (failure to get accounts audited, furnish transfer pricing report, file statements of financial transactions) are converted from penalties into a fee per day with a cap.
- Crypto-asset statement: ₹200 per day for non-filing, ₹50,000 for inaccurate statements not corrected (section 509).

**Prosecution** (corresponds to s.275A to 280): non-production of books and TDS defaults on payments in kind are decriminalised; minor offences carry only a fine; other offences carry simple imprisonment of up to 2 years (or 6 months where the earlier maximum was 2 years); courts may convert imprisonment into a fine.

lesson.heading: Exam approach and common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Always compute penalty on the **tax** effect, not on the income.
- Separate under-reported income into the misreporting and non-misreporting components; apply 200% and 50% respectively.
- For revision questions, test both limbs of "erroneous" and "prejudicial"; an order adopting one of two possible views is not erroneous.
- In reassessment questions, first fix the time limit (3 years, or 5 years for ₹50 lakh and above), then the procedure (inquiry, show-cause, order, notice).
- Do not apply the old 60% rate on unexplained income for tax year 2026-27.

keyPoints: Return filing: section 263 of the 2025 Act; due dates 31 July, 31 August (non-audit business and trusts), 31 October (audit).
Reassessment: 3 years, or 5 years where escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more.
Updated return: within 48 months; additional tax 25%, 50%, 60%, 70%; allowed after reassessment starts with a further 10%.
Appeals: CIT(A) 30 days; ITAT 2 months; High Court 120 days; pre-deposit reduced to 10% of core demand.
Penalty: 50% of tax on under-reported income; 200% for misreporting; immunity now covers misreporting on paying 100% of tax.
Unexplained income taxed at 30% under section 195 of the 2025 Act after the Finance Act 2026.

cases.title: Case: Nair Builders (a firm)
cases.body:
Nair Builders, a partnership firm, filed its return for tax year 2026-27 declaring total income of ₹50,00,000. In scrutiny the Assessing Officer made these additions:

| Addition | Amount (₹) | Nature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Disallowance of excess depreciation (a bona fide claim, fully disclosed) | 8,00,000 | Under-reporting, not misreporting |
| Unrecorded sales found in a survey | 12,00,000 | Misreporting (suppression of facts) |

Assessed income ₹70,00,000. Take the firm's tax at 30% plus 4% cess (31.2%); no surcharge.

questions.prompt: Compute the penalty on Nair Builders for the under-reported income that is not misreporting (the depreciation addition). Answer in rupees.
Compute the penalty on Nair Builders for the misreported income (unrecorded sales). Answer in rupees.
Under the Finance Act 2026 rules, how would the penalty proceedings for Nair Builders be conducted?
options: The penalty is decided in the same common order as the assessment, after hearing
A separate penalty order must be passed within 6 months after the appeal is decided
Penalty can be levied only by the Commissioner (Appeals)
No penalty can be levied once tax is paid
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2026 combines assessment and penalty proceedings into a single common order, after giving the assessee an opportunity of hearing.

questions.prompt: After the Finance Act 2026, Nair Builders can seek immunity from penalty even for the misreported income by paying the tax and an additional amount equal to 100% of that tax, if no appeal is filed.
questions.explanation: Immunity (corresponds to s.270AA) was extended to misreporting cases on payment of tax plus 100% of tax, under sections 478 and 479 of the 2025 Act, subject to conditions such as not filing an appeal and no prosecution having been initiated.

questions.prompt: An updated return is filed after 24 months but within 36 months from the end of the relevant period. Aggregate tax and interest on the additional income is ₹2,00,000. Compute the additional tax payable. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: The additional tax is 60% of aggregate tax and interest where the updated return is filed after 24 months and within 36 months: 60% x 2,00,000 = ₹1,20,000. (25% within 12 months, 50% within 24 months, 70% within 48 months.)

questions.prompt: Income of ₹30 lakh escaped assessment for a year. What is the time limit for issuing the reassessment notice?
options: 3 years from the end of the relevant year
5 years from the end of the relevant year
10 years from the end of the relevant year
No time limit
questions.explanation: The extended 5-year limit applies only where escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more. For ₹30 lakh the limit is 3 years.

questions.prompt: What is the rate of tax on unexplained cash credits for tax year 2026-27 after the Finance Act 2026?
options: Normal slab rates
questions.explanation: Section 195 of the 2025 Act (corresponds to s.115BBE) now taxes such income at 30%, down from 60%. The separate 10% penalty was merged into the 200% misreporting penalty.

questions.prompt: Which are correct statements about revision by the Principal Commissioner of an order prejudicial to revenue? Select all that apply.
options: The order must be both erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of revenue
The assessee must be given an opportunity of being heard
An order passed without making inquiries that should have been made is deemed erroneous
The assessee can apply for this revision
It can be done at any time without limit
questions.explanation: Both conditions must exist, the assessee must be heard, and failure to inquire is deemed erroneous (corresponds to s.263 and its Explanation 2). The assessee applies under the other revision provision (s.264). The time limit is 2 years from the end of the financial year of the order.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: an appeal to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal must be filed within ___ months of receiving the order.
questions.explanation: An appeal to the ITAT lies within two months from the date the order is communicated (corresponds to s.253(3)).

questions.prompt: Which return due date applies for tax year 2026-27 to a partnership firm whose accounts are not required to be audited?
options: 31 August 2027
31 July 2027
31 October 2027
30 November 2027
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2026 moved the due date for non-audit business cases and trusts to 31 August; 31 July remains for individuals filing the simplest returns.

questions.prompt: Explain the procedure for reassessment of income escaping assessment, from information to order, as applicable for the May 2027 attempt.
questions.answer:
(Provisions corresponding to ss.147 to 151 of the 1961 Act; check 2025 Act numbering.)

| Step | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Information | The AO has information suggesting income has escaped (flagged by risk management, audit objection, search or survey material, etc.) |
| 2. Inquiry and show-cause | The AO may conduct inquiry and must give the assessee an opportunity of being heard by a show-cause notice, with the information |
| 3. Order | The AO decides by an order whether it is a fit case, with approval of the specified authority |
| 4. Notice | Notice is issued within 3 years from the end of the relevant year, or within 5 years if escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more |
| 5. Return | The assessee files a return in response; an updated return can now be filed with a further 10% additional tax |
| 6. Assessment | Reassessment order, which may cover other escaped income noticed during proceedings |

The Finance Act 2026 clarifies that the notice is issued by the jurisdictional AO, and penalty is decided in the common order.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between revision in favour of revenue and revision in favour of the assessee.
questions.answer:
- **Prejudicial to revenue** (corresponds to s.263): suo motu by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner; order must be erroneous and prejudicial; within 2 years from the end of the financial year of the order; hearing required; appeal lies to ITAT.
- **In favour of assessee** (corresponds to s.264): on application within 1 year of the order, or suo motu; cannot be used where an appeal is pending or the appeal time has not expired (unless waived); the order cannot be prejudicial to the assessee; no appeal against it, but writ jurisdiction is available.
- Section 263 can cover matters not considered in appeal; it cannot touch issues decided by the CIT(A).

questions.prompt: Summarise the prosecution and penalty rationalisation made by the Finance Act 2026.
questions.answer:
- Assessment and penalty combined into one order; interest on penalty held in abeyance during the first appeal.
- Immunity extended to misreporting on payment of tax plus 100% of tax; not available where prosecution has been initiated.
- Technical defaults (audit, TP report, SFT) moved from penalties to fees per day with a cap.
- Non-production of books and TDS on payments in kind decriminalised; minor offences only fine.
- Imprisonment made simple and capped at 2 years (6 months where earlier 2 years); courts may convert imprisonment into fine.
- Unexplained income taxed at 30%; the separate 10% penalty merged into the 200% misreporting penalty.
- New penalties for crypto-asset statement defaults.

questions.prompt: Which forum hears an appeal against an order of the Commissioner (Appeals)?
options: Income Tax Appellate Tribunal
High Court directly
Dispute Resolution Panel
Board for Advance Rulings
questions.explanation: Orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) are appealable to the ITAT. The High Court hears appeals from the ITAT on substantial questions of law.

chapters.title: General Anti-Avoidance Rule and Tax Planning
chapters.summary: Tax planning, avoidance and evasion; GAAR in Chapter XI of the 2025 Act: impermissible avoidance arrangements, tainted elements, the ₹3 crore threshold and consequences.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Planning, avoidance and evasion
lesson.body:
| Concept | Meaning | Legal status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tax planning | Arranging affairs within the letter and spirit of the law to use incentives the law intends (choosing a regime, claiming s.54-type exemptions) | Legitimate |
| Tax avoidance | Arrangements that comply with the letter of the law but defeat its intent, often with little commercial substance | Legal but countered by SAAR and GAAR |
| Tax evasion | Suppressing income, inflating expenses, false documents | Illegal: penalty and prosecution |

Indian courts have moved between positions. In *McDowell and Co. Ltd v CTO* (1985) the Supreme Court said colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning. In *Union of India v Azadi Bachao Andolan* (2003) it upheld treaty-based planning under the India-Mauritius treaty. In *Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v Union of India* (2012) it looked at the transaction as a whole and held the offshore share transfer not taxable under the law then in force, which led to the retrospective indirect transfer amendment. GAAR, effective from 1 April 2017 under the 1961 Act, gives a statutory basis for the substance-over-form approach.

**Specific anti-avoidance rules (SAAR)** target known schemes: transfer pricing, thin capitalisation (interest limitation), clubbing, deemed dividend, s.50C stamp duty value, bonus and dividend stripping. **GAAR** is a general rule for arrangements that escape the SAARs.

lesson.heading: GAAR in the Income-tax Act, 2025
Thresholds, exclusions and procedure
lesson.body:
Under the rules (corresponding to rule 10U of the 1962 Rules, to be read with the new rules):
- GAAR does not apply where the **aggregate tax benefit** to all parties in a tax year does not exceed **₹3 crore**.
- Excluded: FPIs not claiming treaty benefits; non-resident investors in FPIs; income from transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017.

Procedure:
1. The Assessing Officer refers the matter to the Principal Commissioner.
2. The Principal Commissioner hears the assessee; if not satisfied with the objection, refers it to the **Approving Panel** (a High Court judge as chair, an officer of Principal Chief Commissioner rank and an academic or scholar).
3. The Panel's directions bind the AO and the assessee; the AO passes the order with the Panel's approval.
4. Time limits apply to each stage; the period is excluded from the assessment time limit.

**Tax benefit** includes reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax, increase in refund, reduction in income or increase in loss, including under a treaty.

**Worked example.** A group routes service income of ₹15 crore through a shell entity in a nil-tax jurisdiction instead of the Indian company taxed at 25.168%. Tax benefit = 15,00,00,000 x 25.168% = ₹3,77,52,000, which exceeds ₹3 crore, so GAAR can be considered.

lesson.heading: GAAR and treaties; common mistakes
lesson.body:
Treaty abuse is now also countered by the **principal purpose test (PPT)** brought into many of India's treaties by the Multilateral Instrument (MLI). The PPT denies a treaty benefit if obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of the arrangement, unless granting it is in line with the object of the treaty. GAAR (main purpose) and PPT (one of the principal purposes) can apply together; the CBDT has clarified that where both GAAR and a SAAR apply, the more appropriate provision is used.

Common mistakes:
- Treating any tax saving as avoidance; legitimate use of exemptions intended by law is planning.
- Applying the ₹3 crore threshold per party instead of aggregate for all parties.
- Forgetting that GAAR overrides a treaty under section 159(6).
- Writing "GAAR applies" without naming a tainted element.

keyPoints: GAAR is in Chapter XI of the 2025 Act (section 178 onwards; corresponds to ss.95 to 102 of the 1961 Act); section 179 defines an IAA.
IAA = main purpose of tax benefit + one tainted element (non-arm's length rights, misuse of provisions, lack of commercial substance, non-bona fide manner).
GAAR does not apply if aggregate tax benefit to all parties in a tax year is ₹3 crore or less.
Investments made before 1 April 2017 and FPIs not claiming treaty benefits are excluded.
Approving Panel directions bind both the AO and the assessee.
Section 159(6): GAAR applies even if a tax treaty is more beneficial; MLI adds a principal purpose test.

cases.title: Case: Sundar Group's offshore holding structure
cases.body:
Sundar Group sets up S Ltd in Country X in 2025 with nominal paid-up capital and no employees or office of its own (it uses a corporate service provider's address). S Ltd acquires 40% of an unlisted Indian company, Sundar Retail Pvt Ltd, from the Indian promoter family's Cayman entity in January 2026, funded by an interest-free loan from the Cayman entity. In tax year 2026-27, S Ltd sells these shares and claims that the capital gain of ₹20 crore is not taxable in India under the India-Country X tax treaty, which (assume) gives the right to tax such gains only to the country of residence. The Cayman entity acquired the shares in 2015.

The Assessing Officer believes the main purpose of interposing S Ltd was to obtain treaty benefits.

questions.prompt: Which tainted elements can the Assessing Officer point to in Sundar Group's arrangement? Select all that apply.
options: Lack of commercial substance: S Ltd has no employees, office or business purpose
Location of the asset disguised through an interposed entity
Interest-free funding not ordinarily granted between parties at arm's length
Payment of stamp duty on the share transfer
Use of a corporate service provider's address, which is normal for all bona fide companies
questions.explanation: No substance, disguising location or ownership through a conduit (deemed lack of commercial substance under section 180), and non-arm's length interest-free funding are tainted elements. Stamp duty payment is neutral, and using a service provider's address is not by itself a tainted element.

questions.prompt: Can S Ltd rely on grandfathering for investments made before 1 April 2017?
options: No, because S Ltd made its investment in January 2026
Yes, because the Cayman entity acquired the shares in 2015
Yes, because Country X is a treaty country
No, because grandfathering applies only to listed shares
questions.explanation: The exclusion applies to income from transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017 by the transferor. S Ltd acquired the shares in 2026, so it cannot claim grandfathering, regardless of when the Cayman entity acquired them.

questions.prompt: Assume the gain would be taxable in India at 12.5% (ignore surcharge and cess) if the treaty benefit is denied. Compute the tax benefit claimed by S Ltd. Answer in ₹ lakh.
questions.explanation: Tax benefit = 12.5% x ₹20 crore = ₹2.5 crore = ₹250 lakh. On its own it is below ₹3 crore, but the threshold is applied to the aggregate tax benefit to all parties to the arrangement in the tax year, so any benefit to other group parties is added before testing.

questions.prompt: If GAAR is invoked, S Ltd can argue that the India-Country X treaty prevails over Chapter XI because a treaty overrides domestic law where it is more beneficial.
questions.explanation: Section 159(6) of the 2025 Act (corresponds to s.90(2A) of the 1961 Act) provides that Chapter XI (GAAR) applies even if it is not beneficial to the assessee, so the treaty cannot be used to override GAAR.

questions.prompt: An arrangement shifts service income of ₹15 crore from an Indian company taxed at an effective 25.168% to an entity paying no tax. Compute the tax benefit. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: 15,00,00,000 x 25.168% = ₹3,77,52,000. This exceeds the ₹3 crore threshold.

questions.prompt: An arrangement gives a tax benefit of ₹1.2 crore to Party A and ₹1.5 crore to Party B in tax year 2026-27. Compute the aggregate tax benefit for the GAAR threshold test. Answer in ₹ lakh.
questions.explanation: Aggregate tax benefit = 120 + 150 = ₹270 lakh (₹2.7 crore). It does not exceed ₹3 crore, so GAAR does not apply to this arrangement for that year.

questions.prompt: Which section of the Income-tax Act, 2025 defines an impermissible avoidance arrangement?
options: Section 179
Section 165
Section 206
Section 195
questions.explanation: Section 179 (in Chapter XI) defines an IAA. Section 165 deals with arm's length price, 206 with MAT and 195 with tax on special income.

questions.prompt: Who constitutes the Approving Panel under GAAR?
options: A chairperson who is or has been a High Court judge, an IRS officer of Principal Chief Commissioner rank, and an academic or scholar
Three members of the ITAT
The Assessing Officer, the TPO and the Commissioner (Appeals)
Two CBDT members and a Supreme Court judge
questions.explanation: The Approving Panel has a judicial chair (a current or former High Court judge), a senior tax officer and an academic or scholar with special knowledge of direct taxes, business accounts or international trade.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: GAAR does not apply if the aggregate tax benefit to all parties in a tax year does not exceed ₹___ crore.
questions.explanation: The ₹3 crore threshold is prescribed in the rules (corresponds to rule 10U(1)(a) of the 1962 Rules).

questions.prompt: Which of these is tax planning rather than tax avoidance?
options: A domestic company opting for the 22% concessional regime after comparing tax outflows
Routing a loan through a related shell company to create round-trip interest deductions
Interposing a conduit entity in a treaty country with no substance to claim treaty relief
Sale and immediate buyback of shares at a loss solely to set off a gain
questions.explanation: Choosing a regime the law offers is legitimate planning. Round tripping, conduit entities and wash sales are classic avoidance schemes that GAAR or SAARs target.

questions.prompt: An arrangement is presumed to have the main purpose of obtaining a tax benefit if obtaining the benefit is the main purpose of a step in it, even if it is not the main purpose of the whole arrangement.
questions.explanation: The law treats an arrangement as having a main purpose of tax benefit if the main purpose of a step or part of it is to obtain a tax benefit.

questions.prompt: Explain the consequences that may be applied once an arrangement is declared an impermissible avoidance arrangement, with one example for each of three consequences.
questions.answer:
(Section 181 of the 2025 Act; corresponds to s.98 of the 1961 Act.) The tax consequences are determined as appropriate, including:

| Consequence | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Disregarding, combining or recharacterising any step or the whole arrangement | A series of share transfers through intermediate entities treated as a direct sale by the Indian seller |
| Treating the arrangement as if it had not been entered into | Round trip loan ignored; interest deduction denied |
| Disregarding an accommodating party or treating parties as one | Conduit company in a treaty country ignored; income taxed in the hands of the real owner |
| Reallocating income, expenditure, relief or rebate among parties | Expenses booked in a loss company reallocated to the profit company |
| Treating the place of residence or situs of an asset differently | Asset deemed situated in India |
| Denying treaty benefit | Capital gains exemption under a tax treaty denied |
| Recharacterising equity as debt or the reverse, capital as revenue | Interest on 'loan' treated as dividend, deduction denied |

The consequences are determined in the assessment, following the Approving Panel's directions.

questions.prompt: Distinguish GAAR from SAAR and explain when each is applied.
questions.answer:
- **SAAR** targets a specific, defined scheme with objective conditions (transfer pricing, interest limitation for thin capitalisation, s.50C stamp duty value, dividend and bonus stripping). It applies automatically when conditions are met.
- **GAAR** (Chapter XI of the 2025 Act) is a general, purpose-based rule: main purpose of tax benefit plus a tainted element; it involves a procedure with the Principal Commissioner and the Approving Panel and a ₹3 crore threshold.
- GAAR can apply where SAARs do not cover the arrangement. The CBDT has clarified that the provisions are not mutually exclusive; GAAR can be invoked where the SAAR does not address the abuse fully.
- GAAR applies over treaties (section 159(6)); SAARs apply subject to treaty provisions unless the treaty itself permits them.

questions.prompt: What did the Supreme Court decide in Union of India v Azadi Bachao Andolan, and how does the present law differ?
questions.answer:
- The Court (2003) upheld the CBDT circular that a Mauritius tax residency certificate was sufficient evidence of residence and beneficial ownership under the India-Mauritius treaty, and that treaty shopping was not by itself illegal; it was for the government to renegotiate treaties.
- Present position: India amended the Mauritius and Singapore treaties to tax capital gains on shares acquired from 1 April 2017; GAAR was introduced with a main purpose test overriding treaties; the MLI added a principal purpose test; a TRC is necessary but not sufficient.
- So a conduit structure without substance can now be denied treaty benefits under GAAR or PPT, even with a TRC.

chapters.title: Transfer Pricing and Related International Provisions
chapters.summary: Associated enterprises, international and specified domestic transactions, ALP methods and range, safe harbour and APA after Finance Act 2026, secondary adjustment and interest limitation.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Scope: who and what
Methods and the range concept
lesson.body:
| Method | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Comparable Uncontrolled Price (CUP) | Same or similar product with reliable price data |
| Resale Price Method (RPM) | Distributors who resell without much value addition: ALP = resale price less normal gross margin |
| Cost Plus Method (CPM) | Contract manufacturers and service providers: ALP = cost plus normal gross mark-up |
| Profit Split Method (PSM) | Integrated transactions, unique intangibles |
| Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) | Net profit indicator relative to costs, sales or assets; most common |
| Other method | Any method that gives a price that has been or would be charged in comparable uncontrolled conditions |

The **most appropriate method** is chosen by the functions, assets and risks (FAR) analysis.

**Range and mean** (corresponding rule 10CA):
- If there are **6 or more** comparables (using TNMM, CPM, RPM or CUP), the arm's length range is the **35th to 65th percentile**. If the transaction price is within the range it is accepted; otherwise the **median** is the ALP.
- If fewer than 6 comparables, the **arithmetic mean** is the ALP, with a tolerance: if the transaction price does not differ from the mean by more than **3%** of the transaction price (1% for wholesale traders), the transaction price is accepted.

**Worked example (RPM).** Goods bought from an AE at ₹950 per unit and resold to unrelated customers at ₹1,200. Normal gross margin of comparables: 25% of sales. ALP = 1,200 x 75% = ₹900. For 10,000 units the adjustment is (950 - 900) x 10,000 = ₹5,00,000.

lesson.heading: Compliance, safe harbour and APA
lesson.body:
- **Documentation** (corresponds to s.92D): where aggregate international transactions exceed ₹1 crore; master file and country-by-country reporting for large groups.
- **Accountant's report** (corresponds to s.92E): by the specified date (one month before the return due date of 30 November).
- **Reference to TPO** (corresponds to s.92CA): the AO may refer ALP computation to the Transfer Pricing Officer; the TPO's order binds the AO.
- **Dispute Resolution Panel**: available against the draft order in TP cases.

**Safe harbour (Finance Act 2026 changes)**: software development, IT-enabled services, KPO and contract R&D are combined into a single category of **IT services**, with a common safe harbour margin of **15.5%**; the threshold rises from ₹300 crore to **₹2,000 crore**; approval is automated and can continue for up to 5 years. A safe harbour of 15% on cost applies to data centre services provided by a related Indian entity to a foreign cloud services company.

**Advance Pricing Agreement** (corresponds to s.92CC): unilateral, bilateral or multilateral; valid up to 5 future years with rollback for up to 4 previous years. The Finance Act 2026 targets completion of unilateral APAs for IT services within 2 years (extendable by 6 months) and extends modified returns under an APA to associated entities.

**Secondary adjustment** (corresponds to s.92CE): where a primary adjustment exceeds ₹1 crore, the excess money must be repatriated within 90 days; otherwise it is treated as an advance to the AE and interest is imputed (or the assessee may pay additional tax of 18% plus surcharge on the excess money and be relieved of repatriation).

**Interest limitation** (corresponds to s.94B): interest paid by an Indian company or PE to a non-resident AE (or on debt guaranteed by an AE) exceeding ₹1 crore is disallowed to the extent it exceeds **30% of EBITDA**; the disallowed interest can be carried forward for 8 years. Banks and insurance companies are excluded.

lesson.heading: Penalties and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Penalty rules (as in the 1961 Act): failure to keep documentation or furnish information is 2% of the value of each international transaction; the Finance Act 2026 converts failure to furnish the accountant's report into a fee per day with a cap. A TP adjustment is under-reported income; if it arises from misreporting (for example failure to record the transaction), the 200% penalty applies.

Common mistakes:
- Using the 3% tolerance when 6 or more comparables exist (use the 35th-65th percentile range and the median).
- Allowing a downward adjustment: an ALP adjustment cannot reduce income or increase loss.
- Applying the interest limitation to interest paid to resident lenders not guaranteed by an AE.
- Forgetting that the AE test is about the relationship at any time during the year.

keyPoints: Transfer pricing: sections 161 to 173 of the 2025 Act; section 161 computes income with regard to ALP, section 165 determines ALP.
AE tests include 26% voting power, loan of 51% of book value of assets, guarantee of 10% of borrowings, 90% raw material supply.
6 or more comparables: 35th-65th percentile range, median as ALP; fewer: arithmetic mean with 3% tolerance (1% for wholesale traders).
Finance Act 2026: single IT services safe harbour at 15.5%, threshold ₹2,000 crore; APA up to 5 years plus 4-year rollback.
Secondary adjustment if primary adjustment exceeds ₹1 crore; repatriate within 90 days.
Interest to non-resident AE exceeding ₹1 crore: disallowed above 30% of EBITDA; carry forward 8 years.

cases.title: Case: Zenith India Pvt Ltd
cases.body:
Zenith India Pvt Ltd is a wholly owned subsidiary of Zenith GmbH, Germany. In tax year 2026-27:

| Transaction | Facts |
| --- | --- |
| Import of finished goods from Zenith GmbH for resale | 10,000 units at ₹950 each; resold to unrelated Indian dealers at ₹1,200 each. Comparable independent distributors earn a gross margin of 25% on sales |
| Import of components from Zenith GmbH | 50,000 units at ₹106 each. Five comparable uncontrolled prices: ₹98, ₹100, ₹102, ₹104, ₹106 |
| Loan from Zenith GmbH | Interest paid ₹4.5 crore; Zenith India's EBITDA ₹10 crore; no other interest |

questions.prompt: Using the resale price method, compute the transfer pricing adjustment on the finished goods imported by Zenith India. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Per unit (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Resale price | 1,200 |
| Less: Normal gross margin 25% | (300) |
| ALP of purchase | 900 |
| Price paid to AE | 950 |
| Excess | 50 |

Adjustment = 50 x 10,000 = **₹5,00,000**.

questions.prompt: Compute the transfer pricing adjustment for the components imported by Zenith India. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
Only 5 comparables, so the arithmetic mean applies: (98 + 100 + 102 + 104 + 106) / 5 = ₹102.

Tolerance = 3% of transaction price ₹106 = ₹3.18. Difference = 106 - 102 = ₹4, which exceeds ₹3.18, so the transaction price is not accepted and the ALP is ₹102.

Adjustment = 4 x 50,000 = **₹2,00,000**.

questions.prompt: Compute the interest disallowed under the interest limitation rule for Zenith India. Answer in ₹ lakh.
questions.explanation:
Interest to a non-resident AE exceeds ₹1 crore, so the rule applies.

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Interest paid | 4.50 |
| Allowable: 30% of EBITDA ₹10 crore | 3.00 |
| **Disallowed** | **1.50** |

₹1.5 crore = ₹150 lakh, which can be carried forward for 8 tax years.

questions.prompt: If Zenith India's total primary adjustment exceeded ₹1 crore and the excess money is not repatriated within 90 days, what is the consequence?
options: The excess money is deemed an advance to Zenith GmbH and interest income is imputed
The adjustment is reversed
Zenith GmbH is taxed in India on the excess as dividend
Nothing, repatriation is optional with no consequence
questions.explanation: Under the secondary adjustment provision (corresponds to s.92CE), unrepatriated excess money is treated as an advance and interest is computed on it, unless the assessee opts to pay additional tax on the excess money.

questions.prompt: A Indian company holds 20% of the voting power of a foreign company and has guaranteed 12% of its total borrowings. Are they associated enterprises?
options: Yes, because the guarantee is 10% or more of total borrowings
No, because voting power is below 26%
No, guarantees are not relevant to AE status
Yes, but only if the board is common
questions.explanation: Any one deeming condition is enough. A guarantee of 10% or more of total borrowings makes them AEs even though the voting power is below 26%.

questions.prompt: There are 8 valid comparables using TNMM. The transaction price is outside the 35th-65th percentile range. What is the ALP?
options: The median of the data set
The arithmetic mean
The 35th percentile
The 65th percentile
questions.explanation: With 6 or more comparables, the range concept applies. If the transaction price falls outside the range, the median (50th percentile) is taken as the ALP.

questions.prompt: A transfer pricing adjustment can reduce the income of the assessee if the transaction price was higher than the ALP for a sale by the assessee.
questions.explanation: ALP provisions do not apply where the computation would reduce income or increase loss (corresponds to s.92(3) of the 1961 Act).

questions.prompt: Which changes to safe harbour were announced in the Budget 2026 and given effect for tax year 2026-27? Select all that apply.
options: Software, ITES, KPO and contract R&D combined into a single IT services category
Common safe harbour margin of 15.5% for IT services
Eligibility threshold raised from ₹300 crore to ₹2,000 crore
Safe harbour abolished for IT services
Automated approval continuing for up to 5 years
questions.explanation: The Finance Act 2026 package unified IT services, set a 15.5% margin, raised the threshold to ₹2,000 crore and automated approval for up to 5 years. Check the notified rules for exact conditions.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: specified domestic transactions are subject to transfer pricing only if their aggregate value exceeds ₹___ crore in the tax year.
questions.explanation: The threshold for specified domestic transactions is ₹20 crore (corresponds to s.92BA).

questions.prompt: Which section of the Income-tax Act, 2025 deals with determination of arm's length price?
options: Section 165
Section 161
Section 179
Section 58
questions.explanation: Section 165 deals with determination of ALP (corresponds to s.92C). Section 161 is the charging rule for computation with regard to ALP (corresponds to s.92).

questions.prompt: An Indian company provides software development services to its US parent at cost plus 12%. Operating cost is ₹40 crore. Comparable companies earn net cost-plus margins (OP/TC) of 14%, 15%, 16%, 17%, 18%, 19%, 20%. Compute the ALP using TNMM and the adjustment, and comment on whether the safe harbour would have helped.
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Range**

7 comparables (6 or more), so the 35th to 65th percentile range applies. Sorted: 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20.

- 35th percentile: 7 x 35% = 2.45, rounded up to the 3rd value = 16%
- 65th percentile: 7 x 65% = 4.55, rounded up to the 5th value = 18%
- Median: 4th value = 17%

**Step 2: Test**

The company's margin of 12% is below the range (16% to 18%), so ALP margin = median 17%.

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Operating cost | 40.00 |
| ALP revenue at cost + 17% | 46.80 |
| Actual revenue at cost + 12% | 44.80 |
| **Adjustment** | **2.00** |

**Step 3: Safe harbour**

After the Finance Act 2026, IT services with transactions up to ₹2,000 crore may opt for the safe harbour margin of 15.5%. Revenue at cost + 15.5% = ₹46.20 crore, so the company would have to show ₹1.40 crore more income but would avoid the ₹2 crore adjustment, TPO scrutiny and penalty exposure. The election must be made in time and is automated for up to 5 years.

questions.prompt: What is an Advance Pricing Agreement and what are its advantages?
questions.answer:
- An agreement between the CBDT (with the Central Government's approval) and a person that determines the ALP or the method for determining it for specified international transactions (corresponds to s.92CC).
- Types: unilateral (only Indian authority), bilateral or multilateral (with foreign competent authorities, giving relief in both countries).
- Valid for up to 5 consecutive future years, with rollback for up to 4 earlier years.
- Binding on the person and the tax authorities for the covered transactions unless law or facts change; a modified return must be filed (the Finance Act 2026 extends this to associated entities).
- Advantages: certainty, lower litigation, reduced compliance; the Finance Act 2026 aims to finish IT services unilateral APAs in 2 years.

questions.prompt: Explain the interest limitation rule and the reason for it.
questions.answer:
- Based on BEPS Action 4, it limits base erosion through excessive interest to related non-residents (corresponds to s.94B).
- Applies to an Indian company or a PE of a foreign company that pays interest or similar consideration exceeding ₹1 crore to a non-resident AE, or on debt from a lender guaranteed by an AE.
- Excess interest = total interest minus 30% of EBITDA (or the interest to AEs, if lower) is disallowed.
- Disallowed interest can be carried forward for 8 tax years and deducted within the 30% limit of those years.
- Banks and insurance businesses and certain finance companies in IFSC are excluded.

questions.prompt: When is the arithmetic mean used to determine the ALP?
options: When fewer than 6 comparables are available, or when PSM or other method is used
Always, for all methods
Only for specified domestic transactions
Only when the TPO asks for it
questions.explanation: The arithmetic mean with 3% (or 1%) tolerance applies where the range concept does not: fewer than 6 comparables, or where PSM or the 'other method' is the most appropriate method.

chapters.title: Non-resident Taxation and Double Taxation Relief
chapters.summary: Business connection, significant economic presence and PE; special rates and presumptive schemes for non-residents; DTAA relief, model conventions and BEPS including Pillar Two concepts.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Source rules: business connection and SEP
lesson.body:
A non-resident is taxed in India only on income received in India or accruing or deemed to accrue in India. Deemed accrual is in **section 9** of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (same number as the 1961 Act).

**Business connection** includes:
- an agent in India who habitually concludes contracts, or habitually plays the principal role leading to conclusion of contracts, on behalf of the non-resident (dependent agent);
- an agent who habitually maintains a stock of goods from which deliveries are made;
- **significant economic presence (SEP)**: transactions in goods, services or property (including downloading data or software) with any person in India where aggregate payments exceed **₹2 crore** in the year, or systematic and continuous soliciting of business or interaction with **3 lakh or more users** in India. Only income attributable to the SEP transactions or activities is taxed.

Activities confined to purchase of goods for export, collecting news for transmission abroad, shooting films (for non-resident non-citizens) and certain fund management activities by eligible offshore funds do not create a business connection.

**Royalty, fees for technical services and interest** paid by a resident are deemed to accrue in India (subject to exceptions for use outside India).

**Treaty interaction**: under a DTAA, business profits are taxable in India only if the enterprise has a **permanent establishment (PE)** here. SEP generally does not override a treaty unless the treaty's PE definition is met.

lesson.heading: Special rates and presumptive schemes
lesson.body:
Rates for non-residents (named by 1961 Act section; plus surcharge and cess):

| Income (1961 ref.) | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| Dividend (115A) | 20% |
| Interest (115A, general) | 20% |
| Royalty and fees for technical services (115A) | 20% |
| Foreign company business income | 35% |

Presumptive schemes for non-residents (now within the 2025 Act's presumptive provisions):

| Business (1961 ref.) | Deemed profit |
| --- | --- |
| Services or plant for exploration of mineral oils (44BB) | 10% of receipts |
| Operation of aircraft (44BBA) | 5% of receipts |
| Turnkey power projects (44BBB) | 10% of receipts |
| Shipping business (44B) | 7.5% of receipts |
| Operating cruise ships (44BBC) | 20% of receipts |

The Finance Act 2026 extends the MAT exemption to all non-residents taxed on a presumptive basis.

A treaty rate applies if more beneficial (section 159 of the 2025 Act), provided the non-resident furnishes a **tax residency certificate (TRC)** and the prescribed information (Form 10F under the 1962 Rules). Treaty rates are generally applied without adding surcharge and cess.

lesson.heading: Double taxation relief
lesson.body:
**Bilateral relief** (section 159; corresponds to s.90 and 90A): the Central Government enters into agreements. The assessee may apply the treaty or the Act, whichever is more beneficial (GAAR and other specified provisions apply even if not beneficial). Methods: exemption or credit.

**Unilateral relief** (section 160; corresponds to s.91): where there is no treaty, a resident who has paid tax in a foreign country on income accruing there gets a deduction of the foreign tax at the **lower of the Indian rate and the foreign rate** on the doubly taxed income. The Indian rate is the average rate: tax (with surcharge and cess) divided by total income.

**Worked example.** Resident individual (new regime), Indian income ₹30,00,000, income from Country Z (no treaty) ₹10,00,000 on which ₹2,50,000 tax (25%) was paid.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Total income | 40,00,000 |
| Tax under new regime slabs | 7,80,000 |
| Cess 4% | 31,200 |
| Total tax | 8,11,200 |
| Average Indian rate (8,11,200 / 40,00,000) | 20.28% |
| Relief: 10,00,000 x lower of 20.28% and 25% | 2,02,800 |
| **Net tax** | **6,08,400** |

New regime slabs for tax year 2026-27: up to ₹4 lakh nil; ₹4-8 lakh 5%; ₹8-12 lakh 10%; ₹12-16 lakh 15%; ₹16-20 lakh 20%; ₹20-24 lakh 25%; above ₹24 lakh 30%.

lesson.heading: Model conventions, PE and BEPS
lesson.body:
**Model conventions**: the OECD Model (residence-based, favoured by capital exporters), the UN Model (more source taxation, favoured by developing countries, for example wider service PE and fees for technical services), and the US Model.

**Permanent establishment** types: fixed place (office, branch, factory, workshop, mine), construction PE (beyond a time threshold such as 6 or 12 months), service PE (employees furnishing services beyond a time threshold), dependent agent PE. Preparatory or auxiliary activities do not create a PE.

**BEPS**: the OECD/G20 project produced 15 actions, including Action 1 (digital economy), 4 (interest limitation), 5 (harmful tax practices), 6 (treaty abuse: PPT), 7 (PE avoidance), 8-10 (transfer pricing and value creation), 13 (CbCR) and 15 (the Multilateral Instrument). India has signed and ratified the MLI.

**Pillar One and Pillar Two**: Pillar One reallocates part of residual profits of very large multinationals to market jurisdictions. **Pillar Two (GloBE rules)** sets a **15% global minimum effective tax rate** for groups with consolidated revenue of **EUR 750 million** or more. Mechanisms: a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT) in the source country, the income inclusion rule (IIR) at the parent, and the undertaxed profits rule (UTPR) as a backstop; plus the treaty-based subject to tax rule (STTR). Exam questions test concepts, not computations.

keyPoints: Deemed accrual is section 9 of the 2025 Act; SEP: payments above ₹2 crore or 3 lakh users in India.
Non-resident rates: dividend, interest, royalty and FTS 20%; foreign company 35%.
Presumptive: oil exploration 10%, aircraft 5%, turnkey power 10%, shipping 7.5%, cruise 20%; MAT not applicable to presumptive non-residents.
Section 159 (bilateral relief): treaty or Act, whichever is more beneficial; TRC needed; GAAR applies regardless.
Section 160 (unilateral relief): foreign income x lower of Indian average rate and foreign rate.
Pillar Two: 15% minimum ETR for groups with revenue of EUR 750 million or more; QDMTT, IIR, UTPR, STTR.

cases.title: Case: Kensho Corporation, Japan
cases.body:
Kensho Corporation, a Japanese company with no office in India, has these dealings with India in tax year 2026-27:

| Item | Facts |
| --- | --- |
| Royalty from Indian licensee for a manufacturing patent | ₹50,00,000 |
| Supervision of installation at a client's Indian plant | 4 engineers in India for 5 months |
| Online sales of software subscriptions to Indian customers | ₹3 crore from 4,000 customers |

Assume the India-Japan treaty taxes royalty in the source country at 10%, and the treaty treats a building site or installation project, or supervisory activities connected with it, as a PE only if it lasts more than 6 months. Kensho has a valid TRC and has furnished the required information.

questions.prompt: Compute Indian tax on the royalty received by Kensho Corporation, applying the more beneficial of the Act and the treaty. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Under the Act: 20% plus surcharge and cess. Under the treaty: 10% of gross royalty, without surcharge and cess. The treaty is more beneficial: 10% x 50,00,000 = **₹5,00,000**.

questions.prompt: Does the installation supervision create a PE of Kensho Corporation in India under the assumed treaty terms?
options: No, because the activity lasts 5 months, below the 6-month threshold
Yes, because engineers were physically present in India
Yes, because SEP overrides the treaty
No, because supervision is never a PE
questions.explanation: Under the assumed treaty, an installation project or supervisory activity is a PE only if it lasts more than 6 months. At 5 months there is no PE, so the business profits from supervision are not taxable in India under the treaty.

questions.prompt: Kensho's online sales of ₹3 crore to Indian customers create a significant economic presence under the Act, but the profits are still not taxable in India if Kensho has no PE under the treaty.
questions.explanation: Payments exceed ₹2 crore, so there is an SEP (business connection) under section 9. However, Kensho can choose the treaty, under which business profits are taxable only if there is a PE. SEP does not by itself create a treaty PE.

questions.prompt: Which document is essential for Kensho to claim the treaty rate on royalty?
options: A tax residency certificate from the Japanese tax authority
A no objection certificate from RBI
A certificate from the Indian licensee's auditor
Registration under GST
questions.explanation: A TRC issued by the government of the country of residence is necessary (with the prescribed information) to claim treaty benefits (section 159 of the 2025 Act).

questions.prompt: Mr Iyer, resident (new regime), has Indian income of ₹30,00,000 and income from Country Z (no treaty with India) of ₹10,00,000, on which he paid tax of ₹2,50,000 in Country Z. Compute unilateral relief for tax year 2026-27. Answer in rupees.

A foreign company provides services in connection with exploration of mineral oils in India and receives ₹20 crore in tax year 2026-27. It opts for presumptive taxation (corresponds to s.44BB). Compute its tax including surcharge and cess, with no other income. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Deemed profit 10% of 20,00,00,000 | 2,00,00,000 |
| Tax at 35% | 70,00,000 |
| Surcharge 2% (income above ₹1 crore up to ₹10 crore) | 1,40,000 |
| | 71,40,000 |
| Cess 4% | 2,85,600 |
| **Total** | **74,25,600** |

MAT does not apply to a non-resident taxed on a presumptive basis.

questions.prompt: Which section of the Income-tax Act, 2025 provides relief under a double taxation avoidance agreement?
options: Section 159
Section 160
Section 9
Section 179
questions.explanation: Section 159 covers agreements with foreign countries or specified territories (corresponds to s.90 and 90A). Section 160 is unilateral relief (corresponds to s.91).

questions.prompt: Which are features of the Pillar Two GloBE rules? Select all that apply.
options: A 15% minimum effective tax rate per jurisdiction
Applies to groups with consolidated revenue of EUR 750 million or more
Income inclusion rule applied at the ultimate parent
A qualified domestic minimum top-up tax collected by the source country
A 2% levy on e-commerce supplies
questions.explanation: GloBE uses a 15% minimum ETR, a EUR 750 million revenue threshold, the IIR, the UTPR and QDMTTs. A 2% levy on e-commerce supplies was India's old equalisation levy, not part of Pillar Two.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: significant economic presence exists if a non-resident interacts systematically with at least ___ lakh users in India.
questions.explanation: The notified thresholds are payments of ₹2 crore or 3 lakh users.

questions.prompt: Which model convention generally gives more taxing rights to the source country?
options: UN Model
OECD Model
US Model
All give identical source rights
questions.explanation: The UN Model favours source taxation (wider PE concepts, service PE, more withholding rights), suited to developing countries. The OECD Model favours residence taxation.

questions.prompt: Explain with reasons whether income of a non-resident from each activity is taxable in India: (a) a dependent agent in India who habitually concludes contracts for the non-resident; (b) purchase of goods in India for export; (c) an Indian subsidiary that buys goods from its foreign parent on its own account and resells them.
questions.answer:
| Activity | Taxable? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (a) Dependent agent habitually concluding contracts | Yes, income attributable to the agent's activities | Business connection under section 9; under most treaties a dependent agent PE |
| (b) Purchase of goods for export | No | Operations confined to purchase of goods in India for export do not create a business connection |
| (c) Subsidiary buying and reselling on its own account | No PE of the parent merely by reason of the subsidiary | A subsidiary is a separate entity; it acts for itself, not as agent. The subsidiary is taxed on its own profit and the purchase price is tested for ALP |

In (a), the non-resident may use the treaty if more beneficial, but the agent PE clause (strengthened by the MLI in many treaties) will usually apply.

questions.prompt: Explain BEPS Action 6 and the principal purpose test.
questions.answer:
- Action 6 addresses treaty abuse, including treaty shopping through conduit entities.
- Minimum standard: a statement in the preamble that treaties are not meant to create opportunities for non-taxation, plus a PPT, or a limitation on benefits clause, or both.
- PPT: a treaty benefit is denied if, considering all facts, obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of the arrangement, unless granting it accords with the object and purpose of the treaty.
- Implemented in many Indian treaties through the MLI.
- Interaction: PPT works with domestic GAAR (Chapter XI of the 2025 Act), and section 159(6) allows GAAR to apply even where the treaty is more beneficial.

questions.prompt: How does a resident claim credit for foreign taxes paid, and what is the treatment where there is a dispute about the foreign tax?
questions.answer:
- Credit is claimed under section 159 (treaty) or section 160 (unilateral) of the 2025 Act, in the year in which the income is offered to tax in India.
- The prescribed statement of foreign income and tax (Form 67 under the 1962 Rules; check the new rules) is filed on or before the end of the relevant assessment period, with proof of tax paid.
- Credit is the lower of the Indian tax and the foreign tax on that income, computed source by source and country by country.
- Disputed foreign tax: credit is allowed in the year the dispute is settled, on evidence of settlement and payment, within 6 months of the end of the month of settlement.
- No credit for interest, fee or penalty paid abroad.

questions.prompt: A foreign company earns fees for technical services of ₹1 crore from an Indian company. There is no treaty. What is the tax rate before surcharge and cess?
options: 20% on gross amount
35% on net profit
10% on gross amount
40% on gross amount
questions.explanation: Royalty and fees for technical services of a non-resident are taxed at 20% on the gross amount (corresponds to s.115A), where the non-resident has no PE to which the income is effectively connected.

chapters.title: Equalisation Levy and Other International Taxation Provisions
chapters.summary: The rise and repeal of equalisation levy, indirect transfers, place of effective management, foreign tax credit, advance rulings and Finance Act 2026 incentives for non-residents.
chapters.lawAsOf: Income-tax Act 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Equalisation levy: history and current status
lesson.body:
Equalisation levy (EL) was imposed by the Finance Act, 2016 (Chapter VIII), outside the Income-tax Act, to tax digital transactions of non-residents without a PE in India.

| Levy | Rate | Period | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Online advertisement services by a non-resident to a resident in business or a PE | 6% | 1 June 2016 to 31 March 2025 | **Abolished from 1 April 2025** (Finance Act 2025) |
| Consideration to an e-commerce operator for e-commerce supply or services | 2% | 1 April 2020 to 31 July 2024 | **Abolished from 1 August 2024** (Finance (No. 2) Act 2024) |

So for tax year 2026-27 **no equalisation levy is payable** on any new transaction. Income that was subject to EL was exempt from income-tax (corresponds to s.10(50)); that exemption also ceased with the levy. Past-year disputes and EL returns for earlier periods are still administered under Chapter VIII of the Finance Act, 2016.

The policy gap is now covered by:
- **Significant economic presence** in section 9 (₹2 crore payments or 3 lakh users);
- TDS on royalty and fees for technical services paid to non-residents;
- international work on Pillar One and Pillar Two.

Exam tip: if a question asks for EL on a transaction in tax year 2026-27, the answer is **nil**; explain why and consider whether the income is taxable under section 9 instead.

lesson.heading: Indirect transfer and place of effective management
lesson.body:
**Indirect transfer** (corresponds to Explanation 5 to s.9(1)(i)): a share or interest in a company or entity registered outside India is deemed situated in India if it derives its value substantially from assets in India. Substantial = the value of Indian assets:
- exceeds **₹10 crore**, and
- is at least **50%** of the value of all assets of the foreign company or entity.

Only the gain attributable to Indian assets is taxed:

Taxable gain = total gain x FMV of Indian assets / FMV of all assets

Exemptions: a small shareholder holding (with associated enterprises) not more than 5% of voting power or capital and without management or control rights; transfers in specified foreign amalgamations and demergers; investments in certain Category I and II FPIs. An Indian concern through which value is derived must report the transfer (corresponds to s.285A).

**Place of effective management (POEM)**: a company is resident in India if it is an Indian company or its POEM in the tax year is in India. POEM is the place where key management and commercial decisions necessary for the business as a whole are in substance made. CBDT guidelines apply it only to companies with turnover above **₹50 crore**, and distinguish companies engaged in active business outside India (POEM presumed outside India if the board meets mainly outside India) from others.

lesson.heading: Foreign tax credit, advance rulings and other provisions
lesson.body:
**Foreign tax credit** (under sections 159 and 160 of the 2025 Act): credit is the lower of the foreign tax and the Indian tax on that income; computed income by income and country by country; claimed in the year the income is taxed in India.

**Advance rulings**: the Board for Advance Rulings gives binding rulings to non-residents, specified residents with transactions with non-residents, and others for a determined tax liability, including on whether an arrangement is an IAA under GAAR. Appeals against BAR rulings lie to the High Court.

**Fund management** (corresponds to s.9A): an eligible investment fund's management activity through an eligible fund manager in India does not create a business connection or residence, if conditions are met (minimum 25 investors, no single investor with large stake, fund manager not an employee, etc.).

**Finance Act 2026 incentives** (announced in the Budget):
- Tax holiday up to 2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services to customers outside India using data centres in India; Indian customers to be served through an Indian reseller. Safe harbour of 15% on cost for a related Indian data centre entity.
- Five-year exemption for non-residents supplying capital goods, equipment or tooling to toll manufacturers of electronics in bonded zones.
- Five-year exemption on non-India income of non-resident experts coming to India under notified schemes, if non-resident in the preceding 5 years.
- IFSC units: deduction for 20 consecutive years out of 25; after that, IFSC business income taxed at 15%.
- One-time foreign asset disclosure scheme (FAST-DS 2026) with immunity under the Black Money Act; prosecution immunity for undisclosed non-immovable foreign assets below ₹20 lakh, retrospectively from 1 October 2024.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Computing EL for transactions after its repeal.
- Taxing the whole gain on an indirect transfer instead of the proportion attributable to Indian assets.
- Ignoring the ₹10 crore and 50% tests together; both must be met.
- Assuming POEM applies to every foreign company; the turnover threshold of ₹50 crore applies under CBDT guidelines.
- Treating the IFSC deduction as 10 out of 15 years; it is now 20 consecutive years out of 25.

keyPoints: Equalisation levy: 2% on e-commerce abolished from 1 August 2024; 6% on online advertising abolished from 1 April 2025; nil EL in tax year 2026-27.
Indirect transfer: Indian assets above ₹10 crore and at least 50% of total assets; tax only the proportionate gain; small shareholders up to 5% exempt.
POEM decides residence of foreign companies; CBDT guidelines apply above ₹50 crore turnover.
Foreign tax credit: lower of foreign tax and Indian tax, income by income and country by country.
Finance Act 2026: cloud services tax holiday to 2047, toll manufacturing and expert exemptions, IFSC 20 of 25 years then 15%.
Advance rulings are given by the Board for Advance Rulings; appeal to the High Court.

cases.title: Case: Atlas Holdings BV
cases.body:
Atlas Holdings BV, a foreign company, owns 100% of Atlas India Pvt Ltd. On 15 January 2027 Atlas Global Inc (a non-resident) sells **10%** of the shares of Atlas Holdings BV, with management rights, to an unrelated buyer for **₹100 crore**; its cost was ₹60 crore.

| Particulars (as on the valuation date) | FMV (₹ crore) |
| --- | --- |
| Value of Atlas Holdings BV's shares in Atlas India Pvt Ltd | 600 |
| Value of all assets of Atlas Holdings BV | 1,000 |

In the same tax year, Atlas India Pvt Ltd pays ₹50 lakh to a non-resident social media company for online advertisements targeted at Indian customers.

questions.prompt: Do the shares of Atlas Holdings BV derive their value substantially from assets in India?
options: Yes: Indian assets exceed ₹10 crore and are 60% of total assets
No: Indian assets must be at least 75% of total assets
No: the transfer is of a foreign company's shares
Yes, but only because the buyer is unrelated
questions.explanation: Indian assets of ₹600 crore exceed ₹10 crore and are 60% (at least 50%) of total assets, so both tests are met and the shares are deemed situated in India.

questions.prompt: Compute the capital gain of Atlas Global Inc chargeable in India on the indirect transfer. Answer in ₹ crore.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Sale consideration | 100 |
| Less: Cost | (60) |
| Total gain | 40 |
| Proportion attributable to India: 600 / 1,000 | 60% |
| **Gain taxable in India** | **24** |

The small shareholder exemption does not apply: the seller held 10% (more than 5%) with management rights.

questions.prompt: Compute the equalisation levy payable by Atlas India Pvt Ltd on the ₹50 lakh paid for online advertisements in tax year 2026-27. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: The 6% equalisation levy on online advertisement services was abolished from 1 April 2025. No EL is payable in tax year 2026-27. The payment should instead be examined for TDS and for whether the income is taxable in India under section 9 or a treaty.

questions.prompt: Atlas India Pvt Ltd may have a reporting obligation in respect of the indirect transfer of shares of Atlas Holdings BV.
questions.explanation: An Indian concern through which the foreign entity derives substantial value must furnish prescribed information about the indirect transfer (corresponds to s.285A), with a penalty for failure.

questions.prompt: A resident company earns ₹6,00,000 from Country Y (treaty country) and pays ₹1,20,000 tax there. Its Indian tax on that income at the applicable average rate is 15.6%. Compute the foreign tax credit. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Indian tax on the income = 6,00,000 x 15.6% = ₹93,600. Foreign tax = ₹1,20,000. Credit is the lower: **₹93,600**.

questions.prompt: From which date was the 2% equalisation levy on e-commerce supply or services abolished?
options: 1 August 2024
1 April 2025
1 April 2020
1 April 2026
questions.explanation: The Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 ended the 2% levy for consideration received or receivable from 1 August 2024. The 6% levy on online advertisements ended from 1 April 2025.

questions.prompt: A foreign company with turnover of ₹30 crore has its board meetings in India. Under the CBDT guidelines on POEM, which statement is correct?
options: The POEM guidelines do not apply because turnover does not exceed ₹50 crore
It is automatically resident in India
It is resident only if it has an Indian subsidiary
POEM is decided only by the place of incorporation
questions.explanation: The CBDT has stated that the POEM provisions do not apply to a company with turnover or gross receipts of ₹50 crore or less in a year.

questions.prompt: Which were announced in the Budget 2026 for non-residents and international business? Select all that apply.
options: Tax holiday up to 2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services to overseas customers from Indian data centres
Five-year exemption for non-residents supplying capital goods to electronics toll manufacturers in bonded zones
IFSC deduction for 20 consecutive years out of 25
Reintroduction of the 6% equalisation levy
Five-year exemption of non-India income of eligible non-resident experts under notified schemes
questions.explanation: The equalisation levy was not reintroduced. The other four are Budget 2026 measures; check the enacted provisions and notified schemes for conditions.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: for an indirect transfer, Indian assets must be at least ___% of the value of all assets of the foreign company.
questions.explanation: The two tests are value above ₹10 crore and at least 50% of the value of all assets.

questions.prompt: Who gives advance rulings on income-tax matters for non-residents?
options: Board for Advance Rulings
Authority for Advance Rulings under GST
ITAT
Approving Panel
questions.explanation: The Board for Advance Rulings replaced the Authority for Advance Rulings for income-tax; appeals against its rulings lie to the High Court.

questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Since equalisation levy is abolished, a foreign digital company selling online advertising to Indian businesses now pays no tax in India.' Evaluate this statement for tax year 2026-27.
questions.answer:
**Equalisation levy**

- The 6% EL on online advertising ended on 1 April 2025, and the 2% EL on e-commerce on 1 August 2024. No EL applies in tax year 2026-27.

**Income-tax may still apply**

| Route | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Significant economic presence (section 9) | If payments from India exceed ₹2 crore or there are 3 lakh users, a business connection exists; income attributable to it is taxable |
| Treaty | If the company is resident in a treaty country and has no PE in India, business profits are not taxable in India despite SEP |
| Royalty or FTS characterisation | If the payment is royalty or FTS under the Act or treaty, it is taxable on a gross basis (20% under the Act, or the treaty rate) |
| TDS | The Indian payer must consider TDS (section 393) and Form 15CA/15CB-type reporting |

**Conclusion**: the statement is too broad. Tax depends on SEP, treaty access (TRC, PE, PPT and GAAR) and the character of the payment. Global measures under Pillar One and Pillar Two may also apply to large groups.

questions.prompt: Explain the exemptions from the indirect transfer provisions.
questions.answer:
- **Small shareholders**: a transferor who, with AEs, did not hold the right of management or control and did not hold more than 5% of voting power or share capital of the foreign company in the 12 months before transfer.
- **Foreign amalgamation or demerger**: transfer of shares of a foreign company deriving value from India in a scheme where at least 25% of shareholders of the amalgamating company remain, and no capital gains tax is levied in the foreign country.
- **Specified investment funds**: investments held by non-residents in Category I or II FPIs and similar entities.
- **Threshold**: no taxation where Indian assets do not exceed ₹10 crore or are less than 50% of global assets.
- Even where taxable, only the gain proportionate to Indian assets is taxed.

questions.prompt: Why was equalisation levy introduced, and why was it withdrawn?
questions.answer:
- Introduced in 2016 (6% on online ads) to tax digital businesses that earn from Indian markets without a PE, following BEPS Action 1, as a levy outside the Income-tax Act and so outside treaties.
- Extended in 2020 with the 2% levy on e-commerce operators.
- Concerns: unilateral nature, risk of trade retaliation (a US Section 301 investigation), double taxation (no treaty credit), and overlap with SEP.
- India agreed to the OECD transitional approach linked to Pillar One, withdrew the 2% levy from 1 August 2024 and the 6% levy from 1 April 2025.
- The source-taxation goal now rests on SEP, royalty or FTS rules and international consensus measures.

questions.prompt: What is the taxable gain in India when a non-resident sells shares of a foreign company whose Indian assets are ₹8 crore out of total assets of ₹12 crore?
options: Nil, because Indian assets do not exceed ₹10 crore
Two-thirds of the gain
The entire gain
One-third of the gain
questions.explanation: Although Indian assets are 66.7% of total assets, their value of ₹8 crore does not exceed ₹10 crore. Both tests must be met, so the shares are not deemed situated in India.
